title: Keritot 4
description: Why the blasphemer and conspiring witnesses bring no sin offering, Rabbi Yishmael’s separate lashes for the fat of ox, sheep and goat, Rabbi Ḥanina’s proof that none of the three is learned from the others, “two names” of fat in one lapse, Rabbi Yehuda’s three lashes for sacrificial fat and blood, blood and flesh that combine, Rava’s count of the karet and prohibitions for blood, and Rabbi Illa on second tithe.
topics: 🗣️ Blasphemy is “in the heart” and testimony “through sight”: why neither is an action
🐂 Ox, sheep or goat: does Rabbi Yishmael give separate lashes for each fat?
🔁 Rabbi Ḥanina: why the firstborn ox, sheep and goat cannot be learned from one another
🍽️ Two names of fat in one lapse: notar, sacrificial fat, or two dishes
⚖️ Rabbi Yehuda’s three sets of lashes for sacrificial fat, and for blood
🐍 Blood and flesh that combine: creeping animals and the snake
🩸 Rava counts three karet and five prohibitions for blood
🌾 Rabbi Illa: three sets of lashes for second tithe eaten outside Jerusalem

a1.he: שְׂפָתָיו נֶהֱוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה גַּבֵּי מְגַדֵּף? אָמַר רָבָא: שָׁאנֵי מְגַדֵּף, הוֹאִיל וְיֶשְׁנוֹ בַּלֵּב, אֲבָל בְּעָלְמָא עֲקִימַת שְׂפָתָיו הָוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה.

a2.he: מֵתִיב רַבִּי זֵירָא: יָצְאוּ עֵדִים זוֹמְמִין שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, וְאַמַּאי? הָא ״עַל פִּי״ כְּתִיב בָּהֶן! אָמַר רָבָא: שָׁאנֵי עֵדִים זוֹמְמִין, הוֹאִיל וְיֶשְׁנָן בִּרְאִיָּיה.

a3.he: הָאוֹכֵל חֵלֶב. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״ – לְחַיֵּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל. וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא אַחַת.

a4.he: נֵימָא בְּהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי, דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: לוֹקִין עַל לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת, וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: אֵין לוֹקִין עַל לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת?

a5.he: לְעוֹלָם סָבַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל: אֵין לוֹקִין עַל לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת, וְשָׁאנֵי הָכָא, דִּמְיַיתְּרִי לֵיהּ קְרָאֵי – נִכְתּוֹב קְרָא ״כׇּל חֵלֶב לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ לְמָה לִי? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לְחַלֵּק.

a6.he: וְרַבָּנַן? אִי לָא כְּתִיב: ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: אֲפִילּוּ חֵלֶב חַיָּה בַּמַּשְׁמָע, לְהָכִי כְּתַב: ״שׁוֹר כֶּשֶׂב וָעֵז״, לְמֵימְרָא: דְּחֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז הוּא דְּאָסוּר, אֲבָל דְּחַיָּה שְׁרֵי.

a7.he: שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ! אֶלָּא הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא, דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דְּקָסָבַר: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתּוֹב ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר לֹא תֹאכְלוּ״, ״כֶּשֶׂב וָעֵז״ לְמָה לִי? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לְחַלֵּק.

a8.he: וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: נֵילַף ״שׁוֹר״ ״שׁוֹר״ מִסִּינַי,

a9.he: מָה גַּבֵּי סִינַי – חַיָּה וָעוֹף כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן, אַף גַּבֵּי אֲכִילָה – חַיָּה וָעוֹף כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן, לְהָכִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״, לְמֵימְרָא דְּהָנֵי דְּאָסוּר, אֲבָל חַיָּה וָעוֹף שְׁרֵי.

a10.he: שַׁפִּיר קָא אָמְרִי לֵיהּ! אֶלָּא הַיְינוּ טַעְמָא, דְּקָסָבַר: נִכְתּוֹב ״כׇּל חֵלֶב כֶּשֶׂב לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, אִי נָמֵי: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב עֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ לְמָה לִי? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לְחַלֵּק.

a11.he: וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: אִי כְּתַב ״כָּל חֵלֶב כֶּשֶׂב״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: חֵלֶב כֶּשֶׂב אָסוּר, וְשׁוֹר וָעֵז שְׁרֵי. וְכִי תֵּימָא, מַאי אוּלְמֵיהּ דְּכֶשֶׂב – מִשּׁוּם דְּנִתְרַבָּה בְּאַלְיָה,

a12.he: וְכִדְתָנָא רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָא: לָמָּה מָנָה הַכָּתוּב אֵימוּרִין בְּשׁוֹר וְאֵימוּרִים בְּכֶשֶׂב, וְאֵימוּרִים, בְּעֵז, דִּכְתִיב: ״אַךְ בְּכוֹר שׁוֹר וְגוֹ׳?

a13.he: צְרִיכִי, דְּאִי כְּתַב שׁוֹר, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: כֶּשֶׂב וָעֵז לָא יָלְפִינַן מִינֵּיהּ, דְּאִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: מָה לְשׁוֹר, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה בִּנְסָכִים.

a14.he: נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא בְּכֶשֶׂב וְנֵילַף שׁוֹר וָעֵז מִכֶּשֶׂב – אִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: מָה לְכֶשֶׂב, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה בְּאַלְיָה.

a15.he: נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא עֵז וְנֵילַף שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב מִינֵּיהּ – אִיכָּא לְמִיפְרַךְ: מָה לְעֵז, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה אֵצֶל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה.

a16.he: מִן חַד לָא יָלְפִינַן, נִכְתּוֹב תַּרְתֵּי וְנֵילַף חֲדָא מִתַּרְתֵּי! הֵי דֵין? נֵילַף שׁוֹר מִכֶּשֶׂב וָעֵז – אִית לְהוֹן פִּירְכָא: מָה לְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבּוּ אֵצֶל הַפֶּסַח!

a17.he: לָא נִכְתּוֹב כֶּשֶׂב וְנֵילַף מִשּׁוֹר וָעֵז – אִית לְהוֹן פִּירְכָא: מָה לְשׁוֹר וָעֵז, שֶׁכֵּן נִתְרַבָּה אֵצֶל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה!

a18.he: לָא נִכְתּוֹב עֵז, וְנֵילַף מִשּׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב – אִית לְהוֹן פִּירְכָא: מָה לְשׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב, שֶׁכֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ צַד רִיבּוּי! הִלְכָּךְ לָא יָלְפִי מֵהֲדָדֵי.

a19.he: שַׁפִּיר קָא אָמְרִי לֵיהּ! אֶלָּא לְעוֹלָם טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל כִּדְאָמְרִינַן מֵעִיקָּרָא, דְּאִם כֵּן נִכְתּוֹב ״כׇּל חֵלֶב״ וְלִישְׁתּוֹק. מַאי אָמְרַתְּ, הַאי דִּכְתַב ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ לְמִשְׁרֵי חֵלֶב חַיָּה?

a20.he: הָא כִּי כְּתַב קְרָא – בְּעִנְיָינָא דְקָדָשִׁים, וְדָבָר לָמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ.

a21.he: מִכְּלָל דְּרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: לָא יָלְפִינַן דָּבָר לָמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ? לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא יָלְפִינַן דָּבָר הַלָּמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ, וְהָכָא בְּהָא פְּלִיגִי, רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: לְמֵידִין לָאו מִלָּאו בֵּין מִלָּאו וּבֵין מִלָּאו דְּכָרֵת,

a22.he: דְּ״כׇל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״, מִלָּאו דְּ״חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, דִּכְתִיב בְּעִנְיָינָא דְקָדָשִׁים, וּבְקָדָשִׁים לָא אִית בְּהוֹן חַיָּה, אַף ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״, כִּי כְּתִיב לֵיהּ סְתָמָא לֵיכָּא לְסַפּוֹקֵי בְּחַיָּה, הִלְכָּךְ ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ לְחַלֵּק הוּא דַּאֲתָא, לְחַיֵּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת.

a23.he: וְיָלְפִינַן לָאו דְּ״כׇל חֵלֶב״ וְלָאו דְּ״חֻקַּת עוֹלָם״ מִכָּרֵת דְּ״כִי כׇּל אוֹכֵל חֵלֶב מִן הַבְּהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה״, מָה הָהוּא לְחַלֵּק – אַף הַדִּין לְחַלֵּק.

a24.he: וְרַבָּנַן, לָאו מִלָּאו יָלְפִינַן, לָאו מִכָּרֵת לָא יָלְפִינַן.

a25.he: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הַיְינוּ טַעְמַיְיהוּ דְּרַבָּנַן, כְּדַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרִי לְרַב זְבִיד: ״אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, אַלְיָה דְחוּלִּין תִּיתְּסַר אֲמַר לֵיהּ״ – ״עָלֶיךָ אָמַר קְרָא: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״, דָּבָר הַשָּׁוֶה בִּשְׁלׇשְׁתָּן בָּעִינַן, וְלֵיכָּא״.

a26.he: הִלְכָּךְ: כִּי אֲתָא ״שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז״ – לְמִישְׁרֵי אַלְיָה דְחוּלִּין הוּא דַּאֲתָא. וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, אָמַר לָךְ: אִם כֵּן, לֵימָא קְרָא ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב״, עֵז לְמָה לִי? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לְחַלֵּק.

a27.he: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל לְעִנְיַן קׇרְבָּן שֶׁאֵין מֵבִיא אֶלָּא חַטָּאת אַחַת, מַאי טַעְמָא? דְּלָא דָּמֵי הָדֵין לָאו לְלָאו דַּעֲרָיוֹת.

a28.he: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״וְעָשָׂה אַחַת״ ״וְעָשָׂה הֵנָּה״ – לְחַיֵּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת,

a29.he: שֶׁאִם אָכַל חֵלֶב וְחֵלֶב, שֵׁם אֶחָד בִּשְׁנֵי הֶעְלֵמוֹת – חַיָּיב שְׁתַּיִם, שְׁתֵּי שֵׁמוֹת בְּהֶעְלֵם אַחַת – חַיָּיב שְׁתַּיִם.

a30.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא לְרַב חִסְדָּא: בִּשְׁלָמָא שֵׁם אֶחָד בִּשְׁנֵי הֶעְלֵמוֹת חַיָּיב שְׁתַּיִם, מִשּׁוּם דְּהֶעְלֵמוֹת מְחַלְּקִין. אֶלָּא שְׁנֵי שֵׁמוֹת בְּהֶעְלֵם אַחַת, אַמַּאי חַיָּיב שְׁתַּיִם? הָא בָּעִינַן הֶעְלֵמוֹת מְוחַלְּקִין, וְלֵיכָּא!

a31.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – כְּגוֹן דַּאֲכַל חֵלֶב דְּנוֹתָר, דְּמִחַיַּיב מִשּׁוּם נוֹתָר וּמִשּׁוּם חֵלֶב. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם כֵּן, נִיחַיַּיב נָמֵי מִשּׁוּם קוֹדֶשׁ!

a32.he: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: כְּגוֹן דַּאֲכַל חֵלֶב דְּהֶקְדֵּשׁ, וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא. דְּתַנְיָא: אָכַל חֵלֶב נְבֵלָה, אָכַל חֵלֶב מוּקְדָּשִׁין – חַיָּיב שְׁתַּיִם. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: חֵלֶב מוּקְדָּשִׁין – לוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ.

a33.he: מְחַיְּיכוּ עֲלַהּ בְּמַעְרְבָא: וְנוֹקְמַהּ כְּגוֹן חֵלֶב דְּשׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז, וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא, דְּאָמַר: לוֹקֶה שְׁלֹשׁ!

b1.he: אַלְמָא לָא אוֹקְמַהּ כְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מוֹדֶה הָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל לְעִנְיַן קׇרְבָּן שֶׁאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא חַטָּאת אַחַת, הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לָא מִתּוֹקְמָא, דְּהָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: מוֹדֶה הָיָה רַבִּי יְהוּדָה לְעִנְיַן קׇרְבָּן שֶׁאֵין מֵבִיא אֶלָּא חַטָּאת אַחַת!

b2.he: אֶלָּא אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם בַּר תּאוּטֵנִי: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – כְּגוֹן שֶׁאֲכָלָן בִּשְׁנֵי תַמְחוּיִין, וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, דְּאָמַר: תַּמְחוּיִין מְחַלְּקִים.

b3.he: גּוּפָא: אָכַל חֵלֶב נְבֵילָה – לוֹקֶה שְׁתַּיִם, חֵלֶב מוּקְדָּשִׁין – לוֹקֶה שְׁתַּיִם, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: חֵלֶב מוּקְדָּשִׁין – לוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ.

b4.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שֵׁיזְבִי לְרָבָא: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיבִי קְרָאֵי: ״חֻקַּת עוֹלָם״. ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, ״וְכׇל זָר לֹא יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ״ – הָא תְּלָתָא לָאוִין. אֶלָּא לְרַבָּנַן, מַאי טַעְמַיְיהוּ?

b5.he: קָסָבְרִי: לָאו דְּ״חֻקַּת עוֹלָם״ בְּקָדָשִׁים, וְלָאו דְּ״חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״ בְּחוּלִּין. וּצְרִיכִי,

b6.he: דְּאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא בְּקָדָשִׁים, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: קָדָשִׁים הוּא דַּחֲמִירִי, דְּאָסוּר חֶלְבּוֹ, אֲבָל חוּלִּין – אֵימָא לָא, מִשּׁוּם הָכִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״.

b7.he: וְאִי כְּתַב: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: חֵלֶב דְחוּלִּין הוּא דְּאָסוּר מִשּׁוּם דְּלֹא הוּתַּר מִכְּלָלוֹ, אֲבָל חֵלֶב מוּקְדָּשִׁין דְּהוּתַּר מִכְּלָלוֹ, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: מִדְּהוּתַּר בְּשָׂרָן אִישְׁתְּרִי נָמֵי חֶלְבָּן, צְרִיכִי.

b8.he: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: כִּי כְּתִיב ״חֵלֶב שׁוֹר״, בָּעִנְיָינָא דְקָדָשִׁים כְּתִיב.

b9.he: אֶלָּא מִכְּלָל דְּרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: לָא יָלְפִינַן דָּבָר הַלָּמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ?

b10.he: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא דָּבָר הַלָּמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ, וּבְהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: לְמֵידִין לָאו מִלָּאו וְלָאו מִכָּרֵת, וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: לָאו מִלָּאו יָלְפִינַן, לָאו מִכָּרֵת לָא יָלְפִינַן.

b11.he: אֶלָּא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, ״כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, לְמַאי אֲתָא? מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְהַקִּישׁ, דְּתַנְיָא: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, מָה חֵלֶב לוֹקֶה שְׁתַּיִם – אַף דָּם לוֹקֶה שְׁתַּיִם, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה. וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא אַזְהָרָה אֶחָת.

b12.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא חֵלֶב דְּלוֹקֶה שְׁתַּיִם בְּלָא הֶיקֵּישָׁא, דִּכְתַב בֵּיהּ תְּרֵי קְרָאֵי ״כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, ״כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב״? דָּם נָמֵי בְּלָאו הֶיקֵּישָׁא נִילְקֵי שְׁתַּיִם, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ תְּרֵי לָאוִין ״כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, ״וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכְלוּ בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם לָעוֹף וְלַבְּהֵמָה״!

b13.he: אֶלָּא אֵימָא: מָה חֵלֶב לוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ, אַף דָּם לוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ.

b14.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא חֵלֶב דְּלוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ? דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ הָלֵין תְּרֵי לָאוִין וְלָאו דְּזָרוּת – הָא תְּלָתָא? דָּם נָמֵי!

b15.he: אִיצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הוֹאִיל וְאִיתְמְעִיט דָּם מִטּוּמְאָה – לִיתְמְעִיט מִזָּרוּת, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן הֶיקֵּישָׁא.

b17.he: מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְתַנְיָא: ״כׇּל חֵלֶב וְכׇל דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ״, מָה חֵלֶב מְיוּחָד שֶׁחֶלְבּוֹ חָלוּק מִבְּשָׂרוֹ, וְאֵין מִצְטָרְפִין זֶה עִם זֶה – אַף דָּם, שֶׁדָּמוֹ חָלוּק מִבְּשָׂרוֹ.

b18.he: אוֹצִיא דַּם שְׁרָצִים, הוֹאִיל דְּאֵין דָּמָן חָלוּק מִבְּשָׂרָן – מִצְטָרְפִין.

b19.he: וְהָא מֵהָכָא נָפְקָא? מֵהָתָם נָפְקָא: ״וְזֶה לָכֶם הַטָּמֵא״ – לִימֵּד עַל דַּם הַשֶּׁרֶץ וְהַשֶּׁרֶץ שֶׁמִּצְטָרְפִין זֶה עִם זֶה!

b20.he: אִי לָאו הֶיקֵּישָׁא, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי לְטוּמְאָה, אֲבָל לַאֲכִילָה – אֵימָא לָא, אַשְׁמְעִינַן הֶיקֵּישָׁא לַאֲכִילָה.

b21.he: אָמַר רָבִינָא: הִילְכָּךְ, דַּם נָחָשׁ וּבְשָׂרוֹ מִצְטָרְפִין. מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? הַיְינוּ הֶיקֵּישָׁא! סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: שֶׁרֶץ, דְּאִיתְרַבִּי לְטוּמְאָה – אִיתְרַבִּי לַאֲכִילָה. נָחָשׁ, דְּלָא אִיתְרַבִּי לְטוּמְאָה – לָא אִיתְרַבִּי לַאֲכִילָה, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן הֶיקֵּישָׁא: כׇּל מִילֵּי דְּאֵין דָּמוֹ חָלוּק מִבְּשָׂרוֹ מַשְׁמַע.

b22.he: אָמַר רָבָא: שָׁלֹשׁ כָּרֵיתוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּדָּם. לְמַאי? אַחַת לְדַם חוּלִּין, וְאַחַת לְדַם קָדָשִׁים, וְאַחַת לְדַם הַתַּמְצִית.

b23.he: הָנִיחָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּתַנְיָא: דַּם הַתַּמְצִית בְּאַזְהָרָה, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בְּכָרֵת.

b24.he: אֶלָּא לְרַבָּנַן, הַהִיא לְמַאי אֲתָא? וַאֲפִילּוּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, כָּרֵת נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִן ״כׇּל דָּם״!

b25.he: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: ״דָּם״, מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״כׇּל דָּם״?

b26.he: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא דַּם קָדָשִׁים שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ יוֹצֵא בּוֹ, דַּם חוּלִּין וְדַם הַתַּמְצִית, מִנַּיִן? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״כׇּל דָּם״!

b27.he: אֶלָּא אֵימָא: אֶחָד לְדַם חוּלִּין, וְאֶחָד לְדַם קָדָשִׁים, וְאֶחָד לְדַם כִּיסּוּי.

b28.he: וְאָמַר רָבָא: חֲמִשָּׁה לָאוִין הָאֲמוּרִין בְּדָם לָמָּה? אַחַת לְדַם חוּלִּין, וְאַחַת לְדַם קָדָשִׁים, וְאַחַת לְדַם כִּיסּוּי, וְאַחַת לְדַם אֵיבָרִין, וְאַחַת לְדַם הַתַּמְצִית.

b29.he: אָמַר רַבִּי אִילָא: אָכַל מַעֲשֵׂר דָּגָן וְתִירוֹשׁ וְיִצְהָר – לוֹקֶה שָׁלֹשׁ. וְהָא אֵין לוֹקִין עַל לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת! שָׁאנֵי הָכָא, דִּמְיַיתְּרִי קְרָאֵי –

b30.he: מִכְּדִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא: ״וְאָכַלְתָּ לִפְנֵי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ מַעְשַׂר דְּגָנְךָ תִּירֹשְׁךָ וְיִצְהָרֶךָ״, בִּפְנִים – אִין, בַּחוּץ – לָא, לְמָה לִי דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא: ״לֹא תוּכַל לֶאֱכֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ מַעְשַׂר דְּגָנְךָ וְתִירֹשְׁךָ וְיִצְהָרֶךָ״? לְחַלֵּק.

b31.he: אִי מֵהָהוּא, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בַּעֲשֵׂה, אֲבָל בְּלָאו אֵימָא לָא, אַמְּטוּ לְהָכִי

messages.text: 4a

Continued from 3b: the mishna has the Rabbis exclude the blasphemer from the sin offering, since his sin involves no action. The Gemara has just asked: according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says that the bending of one’s height [in bowing] is considered an action, the twisting of…
…his lips should be considered an action in the case of one who blasphemes.

The case of one who blasphemes is different, since it is primarily in the heart. In other words, the transgression of blasphemy is not the actual speech but the verbalizing of a sentiment. One is not liable to bring a sin offering for such an action, as it is essentially a matter of the heart. But in general, the twisting of one’s lips is considered an action.
messages.quote: considered an action in the case of one who blasphemes

notes.he: עיקר איסורו תלוי ברוע לבו ידע למי גידף הילכך לא חשיב מעשה אבל השתחואה אנו רואין משתחוה לעבודת כוכבים:
notes.en: Since it is in the heart: the essence of his prohibition depends on the wickedness of his heart, that he knew Whom he blasphemed; therefore it is not considered an action. But with bowing, we see him bowing to an idol.

notes.he: עיקר איסורו במחשבת הלב ואין כאן מעשה ומה שמדבר אינו אלא משמיע איסורו אבל כפיפת קומתו היינו עיקר איסורו דאילו היה מדבר במקבל עבודת כוכבים בלא השתחואה לא מחייב דאין עיקר בלב אלא כפיפה היא החיוב. נראה לי:
notes.en: Marginal gloss: Since it is in the heart: the essence of his prohibition lies in the thought of the heart, and there is no action here; what he speaks only voices his prohibition. But the bending of one’s height is the essence of that prohibition [bowing], for were he speaking of one who accepts an idol [as a god] without bowing, he would not be liable [on that count]; the essence there is not in the heart, rather the bending is what makes him liable. So it seems to me.

notes.he: אמר רבא שאני מגדף הואיל ועיקר איסורו היינו במחשבת הלב ומחשבה לא הויא מעשה אבל בעלמא היכא דלא אזלינן בתר מחשבה אמרינן דהקשת שפתיו הוי מעשה:
notes.en: [A printer’s note: “Up to here belongs to 3b.”] Rava said: The blasphemer is different, since the essence of his prohibition is the thought of the heart, and thought is not an action. But elsewhere, where we do not go after thought, we say that the twisting of his lips is an action.

messages.text: All who unwittingly transgress prohibitions punishable by death are liable to bring sin offerings, except for conspiring witnesses, who are not obligated to bring sin offerings, as their transgression does not involve an action.
messages.lead: Rabbi Zeira raises an objection from that which is taught in a different context:

notes.he: בתורת כהנים גבי פר כהן משיח והכי אמרינן אחר שריבינו דברים שהן בעבודת כוכבים ודברים שאינן בעבודת כוכבים יכול שאני מרבה המסית והמדיח ועדים זוממין ת"ל ועשה יצאו אלו שאין בהן מעשה יצאו מכלל חטאת:
notes.en: Conspiring witnesses are excluded: in Torat Kohanim, regarding the bull of the anointed priest. This is what it says there: After we have included matters that concern idol worship and matters that do not concern idol worship, I might think I include the inciter, the one who leads [a town] astray, and conspiring witnesses. The verse states “and does” [Leviticus 4:2]: those in which there is no action are excluded. They are excluded from the category of the sin offering.

notes.he: יצאו עדים זוממין. (בהי) ברייתא היא בתורת כהנים דקתני אי מה עבודת כוכבים שחייבין עליה מיתת ב"ד. אף אינו מרבה אלא את שחייב מיתת ב"ד את מה אני מרבה כגון מקלל אביו ואמו ומסית ומדיח [ונביא] השקר והעדים זוממין ת"ל ועשה יצאו אלו שאין בהן מעשה הלכך אין בהן חטאת:
notes.en: Rabbi Zeira raises an objection: “Conspiring witnesses are excluded.” This is a baraita in Torat Kohanim, which teaches: Or, just as idol worship is something for which one is liable to court-imposed death, so too I include only what carries court-imposed death. What do I include? For example, one who curses his father or mother, the inciter, the one who leads astray, [the false] prophet, and conspiring witnesses. The verse states “and does”: those in which there is no action are excluded; therefore they have no sin offering.

messages.text: But why is that so? It is written with regard to such witnesses: “At the mouth of two witnesses.” They acted through speech, and the twisting of their lips should be considered an action, as they are liable for what they actually said, not for what was in their hearts.
messages.quote: except for conspiring witnesses

verse.he: עַל־פִּי ׀ שְׁנַיִם עֵדִים אוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים יוּמַת הַמֵּת לֹא יוּמַת עַל־פִּי עֵד אֶחָד׃
verse.en: A person shall be put to death only on the testimony of two or more witnesses; no one shall be put to death on the testimony of a single witness.—

notes.he: ונימא עקימת פיו הוי מעשה:
notes.en: But “at the mouth” is written regarding them: so let us say the twisting of their mouth is an action.

notes.he: אין בהן מעשה והא בעדים ע"פ כתי' על פי שנים עדים ונימא דעקימת שפתו הוי מעשה וליחייב חטאת:
notes.en: But why: is there no action in them? Regarding witnesses “at the mouth” is written: “At the mouth of two witnesses.” Let us say the twisting of the lip is an action, and they should be liable to a sin offering.

messages.text: The case of conspiring witnesses is different, since their transgression is primarily through sight, i.e., the important part of their testimony is what they saw, which is not an action.
messages.quote: the twisting of their lips should be considered an action

notes.he: עיקר עדותן בראיית העין שמעידין מה שראו הילכך לא חשיב מעשה:
notes.en: Since they are through sight: the essence of their testimony is what the eye saw, since they testify to what they saw; therefore it is not considered an action.

notes.he: תימה מאי משני ממסית ומדיח ותירץ רבינו נסים במגילת סתרים דכיון דמגדף ישנו בלב כל הני נמי הכי הוא אבל עדים זוממין דאינן בלב אצטריך לשנויי דישנו בראיה ובספרו כתב עדים זוממין הואיל וישנו באם פי' באם לא יגיד ומפרש בפרק שבועת העדות דאין מתחייבין אלא בב"ד ולהכי מעקימת שפתים לא מחייבי דא"כ אפי' חוץ לב"ד נמי והגדתן לחוד דהיינו פיהן לא גרמא להו אבל בעלמא דמחייב ע"פ דבורן לחוד עקימת שפתיו הוי מעשה:
notes.en: Since they are through sight: This is puzzling: how does this answer the inciter and the one who leads astray [whom the same baraita excludes]? Rabbeinu Nissim answered in Megillat Setarim: since the blasphemer is “in the heart,” all of those are likewise; but conspiring witnesses, who are not “in the heart,” needed the answer that they are “through sight.” And in his book he wrote [the reading]: “Conspiring witnesses, since they are [subject to] ‘if’,” meaning “if he does not tell” [Leviticus 5:1]; and it is explained in the chapter Shevuat HaEdut that they become liable only in court. Therefore they are not liable through the twisting of the lips, for if so, they would be liable even outside court; their telling alone, that is, their mouth, does not bring the liability. But elsewhere, where one is liable through his speech alone, the twisting of his lips is an action.

notes.he: שאני עדים זוממין הואיל וישנן בראייה שעיקר עדותן היינו שמעידין שראינו כך וכך ובראייה לית בה מעשה להכי לא ניתנה שגגתן לכפרה דאין בהן מעשה:
notes.en: Rava said: Conspiring witnesses are different, since they are [primarily] through sight: the essence of their testimony is that they testify “we saw such-and-such,” and in seeing there is no action. That is why their unwitting sin was not given atonement [by an offering], since there is no action in it.

messages.text: § The mishna included in its list of those liable to receive karet one who eats forbidden fat. With regard to this, the Sages taught a baraita:

“You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat.” This verse serves to render one liable to receive lashes for each and every one, i.e., one who eats the fat of an ox, and a sheep, and a goat is liable to receive three sets of lashes. This is the statement of Rabbi Yishmael.

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר כׇּל־חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ׃
verse.en: Speak to the Israelite people thus: You shall eat no fat of ox or sheep or goat.

notes.he: מלקות אם אכלן בהתראה אחת:
notes.en: Liable for each and every one: lashes, if he ate them after a single forewarning.

notes.he: על כל מין ומין:
notes.en: To render one liable for each and every one: for each and every species.

messages.text: He is liable to receive only one set of lashes.

Let us say that Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis disagree about this matter, that Rabbi Yishmael maintains one is flogged for violating a general prohibition and the Rabbis maintain one is not flogged for violating a general prohibition. This is referring to the violation of a prohibition that includes several different actions, such as this one, which pertains to eating the fat of an ox, sheep, and goat. The Rabbis contend that one does not receive multiple sets of lashes for transgressing each element of such a prohibition.
messages.quote: only one set of lashes

notes.he: על כל אחד ואחד:
notes.en: One is flogged for a general prohibition: for each and every one [of the things it includes].

notes.he: ואי תיקשי לא לילקי אפילו חדא דחדא מיהא לקי:
notes.en: And the Rabbis hold one is not flogged: and if you ask, then let him not be flogged even once? He is at least flogged once.

notes.he: היינו לאו שבכללות שכולל חלב דשור וכשב ועז:
notes.en: [An editor’s note: it seems one should read “One is flogged for a general prohibition, and this is a prohibition, etc.”] That is a general prohibition, which includes the fat of ox, sheep and goat.

notes.he: ומיהו חדא מיהא לקי:
notes.en: And the Rabbis hold one is not flogged: but he is flogged at least once.

messages.text: Actually, Rabbi Yishmael also maintains that one is not flogged for violating a general prohibition, but here it is different, as elements of the verse are superfluous.
messages.quote: Rabbi Yishmael maintains one is flogged for violating a general prohibition

messages.text: Let the verse write only: You shall eat no fat, and all the individual types of fat would be included. Why do I need the additional terms: “Ox, or sheep, or goat”? Learn from it that the verse serves to separate between them and render one liable to receive a separate set of lashes for eating each type of forbidden fat.

notes.dh: שור וכשב ועז למה לי ש"מ לחלק
notes.he: תימה מאי צריך ג' לחלק בחד סגי:
notes.en: Why do I need “ox and sheep and goat”? Learn from it to separate: This is puzzling: why are three needed to separate? One would suffice.

notes.he: לחלק דנכתב קרא כל חלב לא תאכלו והיה הכל במשמע:
notes.en: Since the verses are superfluous: [they come] to separate; for let the verse write “You shall eat no fat,” and all would be included.

messages.text: And as for the Rabbis, how do they respond to this reading of the verse?

The Rabbis would say that no element of the verse is superfluous, since if it had not written: “Ox, or sheep, or goat,” I would say that even the fat of an undomesticated animal is included in the prohibition. For this reason the verse writes: “Ox, or sheep, or goat,” to say that it is the fat of an ox, or a sheep, or a goat that is forbidden, but all the fats of an undomesticated animal are permitted.
The Rabbis spoke well to Rabbi Yishmael, i.e., their response is persuasive.

notes.he: רבנן דלמישרי חלב דחיה אתו ולא לחלק:
notes.en: They spoke well to him: the Rabbis, [who say] that they come to permit the fat of undomesticated animals and not to separate.

messages.text: Rather, this is the reasoning of Rabbi Yishmael, as he holds: If so, that the verse serves to exclude the fat of only an undomesticated animal from the prohibition, then let it write: You shall eat no fat of an ox, which would be understood as a paradigm representing every type of domesticated animal. Why do I need the phrase: “Sheep or goat”? Learn from it that the verse serves to separate between them and render one liable to receive a separate set of lashes for eating each type of forbidden fat.

notes.dh: אלא היינו טעמא דר' ישמעאל דקסבר
notes.he: נכתוב כל חלב שור למעוטי דחיה וכשב ועז הוו בכלל שור דבהמה נינהו כמו שור אלא למאי הילכתא כתבינהו לחלק:
notes.en: Rather, this is the reason of Rabbi Yishmael, as he holds: let it write “all fat of ox” to exclude undomesticated animals, and sheep and goat would be included in “ox,” since they are domesticated animals like an ox. Then for what law did it write them? To separate.

messages.text: And the Rabbis maintain that if the Merciful One had written only: You shall eat no fat of an ox, I would say: Let us derive a verbal analogy from the word “ox” stated here as a paradigm representing every type of domesticated animal [behema] and the word “ox,” i.e., behema, stated with regard to a mitzva given in preparation for the revelation at Sinai: “Whether it be animal [behema] or man, it shall not live.”

verse.he: לֹא־תִגַּע בּוֹ יָד כִּי־סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל אוֹ־יָרֹה יִיָּרֶה אִם־בְּהֵמָה אִם־אִישׁ לֹא יִחְיֶה בִּמְשֹׁךְ הַיֹּבֵל הֵמָּה יַעֲלוּ בָהָר׃
verse.en: without being touched—by being either stoned or shot; animal or person, a trespasser shall not live.’ When the ram’s horn sounds a long blast, they may go up on the mountain.”

notes.he: למען ינוח שורך (שמות כ״ג:י״ב) מה התם חיה ועוף כיוצא בו דהכי מוקמינן בב"ק בפרק שור שנגח את הפרה (בבא קמא דף נד: ע"ש):
notes.en: And derive “ox” “ox” from Shabbat: “That your ox may rest” (Exodus 23:12). Just as there, undomesticated animals and birds are like it, as we establish in Bava Kamma, in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ et HaPara (Bava Kamma 54b; see there). [Rashi’s text reads the analogy from Shabbat, where the daf reads Sinai.]

notes.he: משבת כתיב הכא שור וכתיב גבי שבת ושורך וחמורך מה גבי שבת חיה ועוף כיוצא בהן דוכל בהמתך יתירא איתרבי דאסור לעשות בהן מלאכה בשבת ויש מלאכה בעופות כגון דש באווזין ותרנגולין:
notes.en: I would say: let us derive “ox” from Shabbat. “Ox” is written here, and regarding Shabbat it is written “your ox and your donkey”; just as with Shabbat, undomesticated animals and birds are like them, since from the superfluous “and all your animals” it was included that one may not perform labor with them on Shabbat (and there is labor with birds, such as threshing with geese and roosters),

messages.text: Rashi and Rabbeinu Gershom read this verbal analogy as drawn from Shabbat (“that your ox may rest”), where the printed text has Sinai.

Just as with regard to the command at Sinai, undomesticated animals and birds are subject to the same prohibition as domesticated animals despite the use of the term behema, so too, with regard to eating their fat, undomesticated animals and birds are subject to the same prohibition as domesticated animals despite the verse employing the example of an ox.

notes.he: אף הכא באכילת חלב חיה ועוף כיוצא בו דחלבה אסור:
notes.en: so too here, with eating fat, undomesticated animals and birds are like it, and their fat is forbidden.

messages.text: For this reason the Merciful One writes: “Ox, or sheep, or goat,” to say that these are forbidden, but all the fats of an undomesticated animal and birds are permitted.
The Rabbis spoke well to Rabbi Yishmael, i.e., their response is persuasive. How could he say the terms in the verse are superfluous?

notes.he: רבנן דלהכי צריכי ולא לחלק:
notes.en: They spoke well to him: the Rabbis, that this is why they are needed, and not to separate.

messages.text: Rather, this is the reasoning of Rabbi Yishmael, as he holds: Let the verse write: You shall eat no fat of sheep; alternatively, let it state: You shall eat no fat of goat. Why do I need the verse to state all three: “Ox, or sheep, or goat”? Learn from it that the verse serves to separate between them and render one liable to receive a separate set of lashes for eating each type of forbidden fat.

notes.he: דליכא השתא ג"ש:
notes.en: All fat of sheep: for now there is no verbal analogy [as “sheep” is not written regarding Shabbat].

notes.he: קסבר ר' ישמעאל א"כ לכתוב קרא כל חלב כשב בלבד ולא מצית יליף מיניה ג"ש משבת דלא כתיב תמן כשב ולא עז. הואיל ונתרבה בנסכים. דכתיב ונסכיהם חצי ההין לפר:
notes.en: Rabbi Yishmael holds: if so, let the verse write “all fat of sheep” alone, and you could not derive a verbal analogy from Shabbat, since neither sheep nor goat is written there. Since it has an increase in libations: as it is written, “and their libations, half a hin for the bull.”

messages.text: And the Rabbis maintain that if the Torah had written merely: You shall eat no fat of sheep, I would say it is only the fat of sheep that is forbidden, but the fat of an ox or a goat is permitted.

And if you would say: In what way is the category of sheep stronger, i.e., more fitting to have its fats forbidden, than the categories of ox and goats, that one would think the prohibition applies only to sheep? The answer is that one might have thought so due to the fact that there is an increased obligation with regard to a sheep’s tail, as it is sacrificed upon the altar, which is not the case with an ox or a goat.

Why does the verse list the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions on the altar with regard to a firstborn ox, and the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions [ve’eimurim] with regard to a firstborn sheep, and the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions with regard to a firstborn goat? As it is written: “But the firstborn of a bull, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are sacred. You shall dash their blood against the altar, and shall make their fat smoke for an offering made by fire.” The “fat” mentioned in this verse is their portions to be burned on the altar.

verse.he: אַךְ בְּכוֹר־שׁוֹר אוֹ־בְכוֹר כֶּשֶׂב אוֹ־בְכוֹר עֵז לֹא תִפְדֶּה קֹדֶשׁ הֵם אֶת־דָּמָם תִּזְרֹק עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֶת־חֶלְבָּם תַּקְטִיר אִשֶּׁה לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: But the firstlings of cattle, sheep, or goats may not be redeemed; they are consecrated. You shall dash their blood against the altar, and turn their fat into smoke as an offering by fire for a pleasing odor to GOD.

messages.text: The Aramaic of the daf reads Rabbi Ḥananya (רבי חנניא) here; the Davidson English reads Rabbi Ḥanina.

These repetitions are necessary, as, if the Torah had written this obligation only with regard to a firstborn ox I would say that we do not derive the halakha of a sheep and a goat from it, as that derivation can be refuted: What is notable about an ox? It is notable in that an ox has an increased number of wine libations, more than those poured with sheep and goat offerings. Therefore, perhaps the additional obligation to burn the sacrificial portions applies only with regard to an ox.

notes.he: חצי ההין יהיה לפר:
notes.en: An ox has an increase in libations: “Half a hin shall be for the bull.”

messages.text: And likewise, if you were to suggest: Let the Merciful One write the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions only with regard to a sheep and we will derive the halakha of an ox and a goat from the halakha of a sheep, that derivation can be refuted: What is notable about a sheep? It is notable in that there is an increased obligation with regard to a sheep’s tail, as explained earlier.

And similarly, if you suggest: Let the Merciful One write the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions only with regard to a goat, and we will derive the halakha of an ox and a sheep from the halakha of a goat, this too can be refuted: What is notable about a goat? It is notable in that a goat has an increased applicability with regard to idol worship, as one who sins unwittingly in the case of idol worship is liable to bring a goat as a sin offering (see Numbers 15:27), unlike one who transgresses other prohibitions unwittingly, for which they are liable to bring a sheep.

notes.he: ביחיד:
notes.en: A goat has an increase regarding idol worship: for an individual.

notes.dh: מה לעז שכן נתרבה אצל עבודת כוכבים ביחיד
notes.he: דכתיב והקריבה עז בת שנתה מה שאין כן בהנך שור נתרבה אצל עבודת כוכבים בצבור דכתיב ועשו כל העדה פר בן בקר וכו':
notes.en: What about a goat? It has an increase regarding idol worship by an individual, as it is written, “he shall offer a she-goat in its first year,” which is not so with these. An ox has an increase regarding idol worship by the community, as it is written, “all the congregation shall offer one young bull,” etc.

messages.text: We cannot derive these halakhot from the halakha of any one of the others, but let the Torah write two of them and we will derive the halakha of one of them from the halakha of the other two.

notes.he: הצד השוה שבהן שהן מין בהמה וחלבו אסור ואימורי בכוריהם קריבים:
notes.en: One from two: from the feature common to them, that they are a species of domesticated animal, their fat is forbidden, and the sacrificial portions of their firstborn are offered.

messages.text: Which is this animal that should not be written? If one suggests we will derive the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions of a firstborn ox from the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions of a sheep and a goat, this derivation has a refutation: What is notable about a sheep and a goat? They are notable in that that they have increased applicability, as they are suitable for the Paschal offering, whereas an ox is not suitable for this purpose.

If one suggests the verse should not write the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions of a sheep, and we will derive its halakha from the halakha of an ox and a goat, this derivation has a refutation: What is notable about an ox and a goat? They are notable in that they have increased applicability as suitable offerings to atone for an unwitting transgression of idol worship, as when a community unwittingly sins with regard to idol worship they bring an ox as a burnt offering and a goat as a sin offering (see Numbers 15:24), while an individual brings a goat but not a sheep.

notes.he: פר בצבור ועז ביחיד:
notes.en: They have an increase regarding idol worship: a bull for the community and a goat for an individual.

messages.text: If one suggests that the verse should not write the obligation to burn the sacrificial portions of a goat, and we will derive its halakha from the halakha of an ox and a sheep, this derivation has a refutation: What is notable about an ox and a sheep? They are notable in that each of them has an increased aspect of applicability with regard to the altar, as the libations for an ox are greater than those for a goat, and the tail of a sheep, but not that of a goat, is burned on the altar.

notes.he: ה"ג מה לשור וכשב שכן יש בהן ריבוי אצל מזבח שור בנסכים וכשב באליה אבל עז אין בקרבנו ריבוי אצל מזבח:
notes.en: This is the reading: “What about an ox and a sheep? They have an increase at the altar”: an ox in libations and a sheep in its tail; but a goat has no increase at the altar in its offering.

notes.he: שור יש לו רוב נסכים שראויין למזבח כשב אליה שלו קריבה למזבח מה שאין כן בעז:
notes.en: For they have an aspect of increase: an ox has more libations, which are fit for the altar; a sheep’s tail is offered on the altar; which is not so with a goat.

messages.text: Therefore, all three cases are necessary, as they cannot be derived from each other.

messages.caption: Rabbi Ḥanina: each attempt to learn the firstborn ox, sheep or goat from the others is refuted.

messages.text: The Rabbis have explained why all three mentions of an ox, a sheep, and a goat are necessary. Consequently, the Rabbis spoke well to Rabbi Yishmael, i.e., their response is persuasive.

notes.he: שפיר קאמר ליה דמצרך צריכין ולא לחלק אתו:
notes.en: He spoke well to him: that they are needed, and they do not come to separate.

messages.text: Rather, the reason of Rabbi Yishmael is actually as we said at the outset, that if so, that one who eats the forbidden fats of all three animals is liable to receive only one set of lashes, let the verse write: You shall eat no fat, and be silent. What did you say in response? That this fact that the verse writes: “Ox, or sheep, or goat,” serves to permit the fat of an undomesticated animal? This is not a valid objection.

notes.he: כדקאמרינן מעיקרא דא"כ דלא לחלק אתו ניכתוב כו':
notes.en: Actually: as we said at the outset, that if so, that they do not come to separate, let it write, etc.

messages.text: When the verse concerning forbidden fat is written it is in the context of sacrificial animals, since the subsequent verse concerning the prohibition against eating forbidden fat states: “For whoever eats the fat of the animal of which men present an offering of fire to the Lord, even the soul that eats it shall be cut off from his people.” The verse categorizes an animal whose fat one may not eat as an “animal of which men present an offering of fire to the Lord,” i.e., offerings.

verse.he: כִּי כׇּל־אֹכֵל חֵלֶב מִן־הַבְּהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיב מִמֶּנָּה אִשֶּׁה לַיהֹוָה וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הָאֹכֶלֶת מֵעַמֶּיהָ׃
verse.en: If anyone eats the fat of animals from which offerings by fire may be made to GOD, the person who eats it shall be cut off from kin.

notes.dh: הא כי כתיב קרא בעניינא דקדשים כתיב
notes.he: דכתיב (ויקרא ז) כי כל אוכל חלב מן הבהמה וגו' והואיל ובעניינא דקדשים כתיב ודאי אין חיה נוהגת בהו הלכך לא איצטריך שור וכבש למישרי חיה:
notes.en: But when the verse is written, it is written in the context of sacrificial animals: as it is written (Leviticus 7[:25]), “For whoever eats the fat of the animal…”. Since it is written in the context of sacrificial animals, undomesticated animals certainly do not apply there; therefore “ox and sheep” is not needed to permit undomesticated animals.

messages.text: And one of the thirteen hermeneutical principles is: A matter is derived from its context, i.e., one interprets a verse according to the context in which it is written. Since offerings may be brought only from domesticated, not undomesticated, animals, the prohibition against eating forbidden fat applies only to such animals.

notes.he: מה חיה בקדשים ליתא אף באיסור חלב ליתא:
notes.en: And a matter is learned from its context: just as there are no undomesticated animals among sacrificial animals, so too there are none in the prohibition of fat.

notes.he: ושור וכשב ועז לא אתי אלא לחלק:
notes.en: And “ox and sheep and goat” comes only to separate.

messages.text: Can one conclude by inference that the Rabbis maintain we do not derive halakhot by employing the hermeneutical principle of: A matter is derived from its context? This cannot be correct, as it is an accepted basic principle of exegesis.

notes.he: לא ילפינן לאו דכל חלב מעניינו בתמיה:
notes.en: By inference the Rabbis hold: that we do not derive the prohibition of “all fat” from its context? [Said] in astonishment.

notes.he: מכלל דרבנן דאמרי דצריכי סברי לא ילפינן דבר מעניינו והא היינו אחת מי"ג מדות שהתורה נדרשת:
notes.en: By inference the Rabbis, who say they are needed, hold we do not derive a matter from its context? But that is one of the thirteen principles by which the Torah is expounded!

messages.text: No, everyone agrees that we do derive halakhot by employing the hermeneutical principle of: A matter is derived from its context, and here it is about this issue that they disagree: Rabbi Yishmael maintains that we derive the halakhot of one prohibition from the halakhot of another prohibition, and this applies whether it is from a standard prohibition, whose transgression results in the punishment of lashes, or whether from a prohibition whose transgression results in the punishment of karet.
messages.quote: the Rabbis maintain we do not derive

notes.dh: דכולי עלמא ילפינן דבר למד מעניינו
notes.he: בעלמא אבל הכא לאו עניינו דהאי לאו והאי כרת:
notes.en: Everyone derives a matter learned from its context: in general. But here it is not its context, since this one is a prohibition and that one is karet.

notes.he: גירסא זו הכתובה בספרים משובשת היא ועל ידי פרשנים טועין שלא היו בקיאין בשמועה ופירשוה בשיבוש בתוך הגירסא וכך הצעה ולא יותר והכא בהא קמיפלגי מר סבר למידין לאו מלאו ולאו מכרת ומר סבר לאו מלאו ילפינן לאו מכרת לא ילפינן והכי פירושא ר' ישמעאל סבר למידין דבר מעניינו בין לאו מלאו בין לאו מכרת:
notes.en: And here they disagree about this, etc.: the reading written in the books here is corrupt, the work of mistaken commentators who were not expert in the passage and wrote their garbled explanation into the text. The arrangement is this and no more: “And here they disagree about this: one Sage holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition and a prohibition from karet, and the other Sage holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition but do not derive a prohibition from karet.” And this is its explanation: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive a matter from its context, whether a prohibition from a prohibition or a prohibition from karet.

notes.he: לאו דכל חלב שור מן לאו דחקת עולם דחוקת עולם ודאי בענינא דקדשים כתב דלפניו ולאחריו אינו מדבר אלא בקדשים אבל האי כל חלב שור לא כתיב בענינא דקדשים כל כך דהא סמיך ליה וחלב נבלה וחלב טרפה דהיינו דחולין וכיון דילפי' לאו דכל חלב מהלאו דחקת עולם דכתיב בקדשים (אבל האי כל חלב שור לא כתיב בענינא דקדשים דלית בהו חיה) אפי' כתיב כל חלב לא תאכלו סתמא (דלא) [ולא היה] כתיב שור וכשב ועז לא איכא לספוקי בחלב דחיה דהא ליתא בקדשים:
notes.en: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive: the prohibition of “all fat of ox” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute.” “A perpetual statute” is certainly written in the context of sacrificial animals, since before it and after it the passage speaks only of sacrificial animals; but “all fat of ox” is not written so fully in the context of sacrificial animals, since next to it is “and the fat of a carcass and the fat of a torn animal,” which are non-sacred. And since we derive the prohibition of “all fat” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” which is written about sacrificial animals (but this “all fat of ox” is not written in the context of sacrificial animals, among which there are no undomesticated animals), even had it written “You shall eat no fat” without specification [and not] written “ox and sheep and goat,” there would be no doubt about the fat of undomesticated animals, since they are not among sacrificial animals.

messages.text: Accordingly, the prohibition of: “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat,” can be derived from the prohibition of: “It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings, that you shall eat neither fat nor blood,” which is written with regard to the matter of sacrificial animals. And there are no undomesticated animals in the category of sacrificial animals.

verse.he: חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם כׇּל־חֵלֶב וְכׇל־דָּם לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ׃ {פ}
verse.en: It is a law for all time throughout the ages, in all your settlements: you must not eat any fat or any blood.

messages.text: So too, with regard to the prohibition of: “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat,” when the verse writes it without further specification, there is no reason to be uncertain whether or not it is referring also to undomesticated animals. Therefore, the phrase “ox, or sheep, or goat” comes to separate, i.e., to render one liable for eating the forbidden fat of each and every one of them.

notes.he: למלקות הוא דאתא וחייב על כל אחת ואחת איסורא בעלמא אבל לחלק מלקיות לכריתות אכתי לא ידעינן אלא ילפינן לאו דכל חלב ולאו דחוקת עולם מן כרת דכתיב כי כל אוכל חלב מן הבהמה וגו':
notes.en: Therefore “ox and sheep and goat” is to separate: it comes for lashes, and he is liable for each and every one. [An editor’s note: it seems from this that our Rabbi had a different reading here: that the Rabbis hold we derive from the superfluous words only a mere prohibition, that he transgresses three prohibitions, but not for lashes.] A mere prohibition; but to separate the lashes [like] the karet penalties we still do not know. Rather, we derive the prohibition of “all fat” and the prohibition of “a perpetual statute” from the karet, as it is written, “For whoever eats the fat of the animal…”.

messages.text: All this teaches only that a separate prohibition applies to each type of animal. And with regard to the liability to receive lashes for eating each one we derive the prohibition of: “You shall eat no fat,” and the prohibition of: “It shall be a perpetual statute,” from the example of karet stated in the verse: “For anyone who eats the fat of the domesticated animal, of which people present an offering of fire to the Lord, the soul that eats it shall be cut off from its people.”

notes.he: לחייב על בהמה ובהמה הראויה להקרבה:
notes.en: Just as that one is to separate: to render one liable for each animal fit to be offered.

messages.text: Just as that verse serves to separate and teach that if one unwittingly ate the fat of an ox, a goat, and a sheep he is liable to bring a sin offering for each one, so too, this verse serves to separate and teach that one is liable to receive lashes for eating the fat of each one.

notes.he: לאו דכל חלב ושור דחולין לחלק מלקות וכרת לכל אחת:
notes.en: So too this one: the prohibition of “all fat,” and “ox” of non-sacred animals, is to separate lashes and karet for each one.

notes.he: לישנא אחרינא ר' ישמעאל סבר למידין לאו דחקת עולם דכתיב בעניניה (דקרא) [דקדשים] דמההוא לא מצית לרבויי חלב חיה מקדשי' דלית בהו חיה ומכל חלב שור נמי לא מצית לרבויי חלב חיה דאפי' כתיב נמי סתמא בלא פרטי ליכא לספוקי בחיה דליתסר חלבה דהא ילפינן האי כל חלב דשור מחלב דכרת מה בכרת פרט בהמה ולא חיה אף כאן נמי הלכך שור וכשב ועז לחלק:
notes.en: Another version: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive [from] the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” written in the context of sacrificial animals, from which you cannot include the fat of undomesticated animals, since there are no undomesticated animals among sacrificial animals. And from “all fat of ox” too you cannot include the fat of undomesticated animals, for even had it been written without specifics, there would be no doubt about undomesticated animals that their fat is forbidden, since we derive this “all fat of ox” from the fat of the karet: just as with the karet it specifies a domesticated animal and not an undomesticated one, so too here. Therefore “ox and sheep and goat” is to separate.

messages.text: And the Rabbis maintain we derive the halakhot of one standard prohibition from the halakhot of another standard prohibition, but we do not derive the halakhot of a standard prohibition from the halakhot of a prohibition whose transgression results in the punishment of karet.

notes.he: לאו מלאו למידין זה מזה כשהן בפרשה אחת דבר למד מעניינו כי ההיא דבשר בחלב השנויה בפ' כל הבשר (חולין קטו:) לא תאכלנו בבשר בחלב הכתוב מדבר אבל לאו מכרת כעין הכא לא ילפינן דבר למד מעניינו הלכך אי לא כתיב שור וכשב ועז ה"א חיה במשמע:
notes.en: And the Rabbis hold: a prohibition from a prohibition, we derive one from the other when they are in one passage, as a matter learned from its context, like the case of meat in milk taught in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 115b): “You shall not eat it”: the verse speaks of meat in milk. But a prohibition from karet, as here, we do not derive as a matter learned from its context. Therefore, had “ox and sheep and goat” not been written, I would have said undomesticated animals are included.

notes.he: אמרי מכרת דבעית למילף מיניה לחלק למלקיות לא מצית ילפת דלאו מלאו ילפינן דדמי ליה והיינו דבר למד מענינו וכדאמר בפרק כל הבשר לא תאכלנו למען ייטב לך. בבשר בחלב הכתוב מדבר או אינו אלא בשאר איסורים אמרת צא ולמד מי"ג מדות דבר למד מענינו במה הכתוב מדבר לא תאכלנו דלמעלה בב' מינין דכתיב לא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר אף כאן ב' מינין היינו בשר בחלב אלמא לאו מלאו ילפינן דדמי ליה לאו מכרת לא ילפינן והלכך אינו חייב אלא אחת:
notes.en: And the Rabbis: say that from the karet, from which you want to derive separate lashes, you cannot derive, since we derive a prohibition from a prohibition that resembles it, and that is “a matter learned from its context,” as it says in the chapter Kol HaBasar: “You shall not eat it, that it may be well with you”: the verse speaks of meat in milk. Or is it only about other prohibitions? You said: go out and learn from the thirteen principles: a matter learned from its context. What is the verse speaking of? “You shall not eat it” above is about two kinds, as it is written, “you shall not eat the life with the flesh”; so too here, two kinds, that is meat in milk. Evidently we derive a prohibition from a prohibition that resembles it, but we do not derive a prohibition from karet; therefore he is liable only once.

notes.he: ורבנן לאו מלאו ילפי כו':
notes.en: And the Rabbis derive a prohibition from a prohibition, etc.

messages.text: Rashi says the longer wording found in the books here is corrupt, written into the text by mistaken commentators. His reading is only: “One Sage holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition and a prohibition from karet; the other holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition but not a prohibition from karet.”
And if you wish, say instead that this is the reason of the Rabbis:

notes.he: משום דהאי שור וכשב ועז מיבעי להו לכדרב מרי:
notes.en: And if you wish, say the reason of the Rabbis: is that they need this “ox and sheep and goat” for the teaching of Rav Mari.

messages.text: If that is so, that a sheep tail is categorized as fat by the verses and is included in the portions of an offering for which one is liable for the misuse of consecrated property, then the tail of a non-sacred animal should be prohibited for consumption as forbidden fat.
messages.lead: As Rav Mari said to Rav Zevid when asked about a different issue:

notes.he: דחלב איקרי בפרק כל הבשר (חולין קיז.):
notes.en: The tail of a non-sacred animal should be prohibited: since it is called fat, in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 117a).

messages.text: With regard to your claim, the verse states concerning forbidden fat: “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat.” This teaches that for the prohibition against eating forbidden fat to take effect we require an item that is found equally in all three types of animals, an ox, and a sheep, and a goat, and that is not the case here. Since an ox and goat do not have tails, the tail is not prohibited even in the case of a sheep.
messages.quote: tail of a non-sacred animal should be prohibited

notes.he: שנקרא חלב בשלשתן ואליה לא איקרי חלב אלא בכשב:
notes.en: That is equal in all three: that is called fat in all three; and the tail is called fat only in a sheep.

notes.he: היינו טעמא דלא אתי לחלק דמיבעי להו שור וכשב ועז להאי דרשא לכדאמר ליה רב מרי לרב זביד בפרק כל הבשר אלא מעתה כיון דמכל חלב קא מרבית אליה אליה דחולין תיתסר באכילה א"ל עליך אמר קרא כל חלב שור וכשב ועז לא תאכלו חלב גמור השוה בשלשתן דסליק באימורין אסור לאפוקי אליה דלא שוה בשלשתן דליתא אלא בכבש להכי כתיבי למישרא אליה דחולין:
notes.en: And if you wish, say [of] the Rabbis: this is the reason it does not come to separate, since they need “ox and sheep and goat” for this exposition, as Rav Mari said to Rav Zevid in the chapter Kol HaBasar: But now, since you include the tail from “all fat,” the tail of a non-sacred animal should be forbidden to eat! He said to him: Regarding you, the verse states, “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat”: complete fat, equal in all three, which goes up among the sacrificial portions, is forbidden, excluding the tail, which is not equal in all three, as it exists only in a sheep. That is why they are written: to permit the tail of non-sacred animals.

messages.text: Therefore, the same applies with regard to the issue at hand: When the verse “ox, or sheep, or goat” comes, it comes to permit consumption of the tail of a non-sacred animal, and one cannot learn from here that a separate prohibition applies to each type of forbidden fat.

And Rabbi Yishmael could say to you in response: If so, let the verse state: You shall eat no fat of ox or sheep; why do I need the mention of a goat? Learn from it that the verse serves to separate between them and render one liable to receive lashes for eating each type of forbidden fat.

notes.dh: א"כ נכתוב כל חלב שור וכשב
notes.he: ומהתם ממעיטנא אליה דבעינן דבר השוה בשניהן:
notes.en: If so, let it write “all fat of ox and sheep”: and from there I would exclude the tail, since we require something equal in both of them.

notes.he: א"כ לטעמיך לימא קרא כל חלב שור וכשב חלב השוה בשניהם ואליה אינה שוה בשניהם ועז למאי כתביה לחלק:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yishmael would say to you: if so, by your reasoning, let the verse say “all fat of ox and sheep,” fat equal in both of them, and the tail is not equal in both. For what did it write goat? To separate.

notes.he: אמרי איידי דכתיב שור וכשב כתיב עז:
notes.en: And the Rabbis: say that since it wrote ox and sheep, it wrote goat as well.

messages.text: Although Rabbi Yishmael maintains that one who unwittingly eats the fat of an ox, a sheep, and a goat is liable to receive a separate set of lashes for each one, he concedes with regard to bringing an offering that if he ate those types of forbidden fat in a single lapse of awareness he brings only one sin offering.

notes.he: אע"ג [דנפק"ל מקרא] לחייב על כל אחד הני מילי לענין מלקות אבל לענין קרבן אין מביא אלא חטאת אחת דלא דמי האי לאו דכתיב אשלשתן להא לאו דעריות דהתם כתיב לאו אכל ערוה וערוה:
notes.en: Rabbi Yishmael concedes: even though [he derives from a verse] to render one liable for each one, that applies to lashes; but regarding an offering he brings only one sin offering, since this prohibition, written for all three together, does not resemble the prohibition of forbidden relations, where a prohibition is written for each and every forbidden relative.

messages.text: What is the reason? The reason is that this prohibition is not similar to the prohibition of those with whom relations are forbidden. As derived in the Gemara on 2b, one who unwittingly engages in intercourse with many women to whom he is forbidden is liable to bring a sin offering for each act. In that context the verse states a separate prohibition for each forbidden relative, whereas in this case there is a single prohibition that applies to the forbidden fat of all domesticated animals.
messages.quote: brings only one sin offering

notes.he: להכי נקט עריות דאיכא מילי טובא ואיכא לאו בכל חדא:
notes.en: The prohibition of forbidden relations: he mentions forbidden relations because there are many cases there, with a prohibition for each one.

messages.text: § With regard to the sin offering required of one who transgresses the prohibition against eating forbidden fat, the Sages taught in a baraita:

The verse states: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying: A soul that sins in error, from all the commandments of God that may not be performed, and from one of them.” This phrase should be interpreted as though it states: And performs one, and again states: And performs them, i.e., it serves to render one liable to bring a sin offering for each and every transgression.

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר נֶפֶשׁ כִּי־תֶחֱטָא בִשְׁגָגָה מִכֹּל מִצְוֺת יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא תֵעָשֶׂינָה וְעָשָׂה מֵאַחַת מֵהֵנָּה׃
verse.en:
Speak to the Israelite people thus:
When a person unwittingly incurs guilt in regard to any of GOD’s commandments about things not to be done, and does one of them—

notes.he: משמע מאחת חייב הנה כמה חטאות:
notes.en: “From one of them” [me’aḥat mehena]: implies that for one he is liable; “them,” several sin offerings.

notes.he: היינו אחת שהיא הנה:
notes.en: “And does one” and “and does them”: that is, one that is them [several].

messages.text: This teaches that if one ate forbidden fat and again ate forbidden fat, if it was from one category, i.e., the same type of forbidden fat, and he ate it in two lapses of awareness, that is, he was made aware of his sin after the first instance of consumption and then again ate unwittingly, he is liable to bring two sin offerings. If he ate forbidden fat from two categories, as the Gemara will soon explain, in one lapse of awareness, he is likewise liable to bring two sin offerings.

notes.he: שני זיתי חלב:
notes.en: Fat and fat: two olive-bulks of fat.

notes.he: חלב הכליות או חלב הדקין שם אחד בהעלם אחד ל"ג:
notes.en: One name: the fat of the kidneys, or the fat of the intestines, is one name. We do not read “in one lapse of awareness” [here].

notes.he: כזית משעל הכוליא וכזית משעל הדקין:
notes.en: Two names: an olive-bulk from upon the kidney and an olive-bulk from upon the intestines.

notes.dh: לחייב על כל אחת ואחת שאם אכל חלב וחלב שם אחד
notes.he: כלומר שתי זיתי חלב ממין אחד בשתי העלמות חייב שתים או ב' שמות כגון כזית מחלב שעל גבי הקרב וכזית ממעל הדקין או כזית מחלב שור וכזית מחלב כבש בהעלם אחת חייב שתים:
notes.en: To render one liable for each and every one, that if he ate fat and fat of one name: that is, two olive-bulks of fat of one species in two lapses of awareness, he is liable to two; or two names, such as an olive-bulk of the fat on the innards and an olive-bulk from upon the intestines, or an olive-bulk of ox fat and an olive-bulk of sheep fat, in one lapse of awareness, he is liable to two.

messages.text: @Rav Ḥisda Granted, one who ate forbidden fat from one category in two lapses of awareness is liable to bring two sin offerings, as this is due to the fact that the lapses of awareness separate between his transgressions; each time he becomes aware of his transgression he is liable to bring another sin offering.
messages.quote: two categories, in one lapse of awareness

notes.he: דכיון דנודע לו בינתים הרי הן שתי שגגות וחטאת בידיעה תלה רחמנא דכתיב (ויקרא ד) או הודע אליו:
notes.en: Since lapses of awareness separate: since he became aware in between, these are two errors, and the Merciful One made the sin offering depend on awareness, as it is written (Leviticus 4[:23]): “Or if his sin be made known to him.”

messages.text: But in a case where he ate forbidden fat from two categories in one lapse of awareness, why is he liable to bring two sin offerings? We require separate lapses of awareness and that is not the case here.

notes.dh: אלא ב' שמות בהעלם אחת אמאי חייב שתים
notes.he: הא ליכא לא חילוק העלמות ולא חילוק לאוין דהא ליכא אלא אחד בחולין כל חלב שור וכשב ועז כגון דאכל חלב דנותר דאיכא ב' לאוין:
notes.en: But two names in one lapse of awareness, why is he liable to two? There is neither a division of lapses nor a division of prohibitions, since with non-sacred animals there is only one, “all fat of ox, or sheep, or goat.” [Rav Ḥisda answers:] for example, where he ate fat of notar, where there are two prohibitions.

messages.text: Here we are dealing with a case where he ate forbidden fat left over from an offering after the time allotted for its consumption [notar], as he is liable due to eating notar and is also liable due to eating forbidden fat. These are the two categories mentioned in the baraita.

notes.he: דאיכא שתי שגגות משתי כריתות חלב ונותר וחייב שתי חטאות:
notes.en: Fat of notar: as there are two errors involving two karet prohibitions, fat and notar, and he is liable to two sin offerings.

messages.text: If so, that the case involves more than one prohibition, let him be liable due to eating sacrificial food as well, and he should be liable to bring a guilt offering for the unwitting misuse of consecrated property (see Leviticus 5:14–16).
messages.quote: he is liable due to eating notar and is also liable due to eating forbidden fat

notes.he: אשם מעילות:
notes.en: Let him be liable on account of the sacred as well: a guilt offering for misuse [of consecrated property].

notes.he: דנותר היינו דכתיב כל זר לא יאכל קדש דאפי' כהן לגבי נותר זר הוי והיינו תלתא לאוין:
notes.en: If so, let him be liable on account of the sacred as well: since of notar it is written, “No non-priest shall eat of the sacred,” for even a priest is a non-priest with regard to notar; and that makes three prohibitions.

messages.text: Here we are dealing with a case where he ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, and this ruling is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who renders one liable to bring two sin offerings for eating forbidden fat of sacrificial food.

notes.dh: אלא אמר רב ששת כגון שאכל חלב דקודש
notes.he: ולעולם משום חלב חייב שתים ולהכי לא חשיב אשם מעילות אלא של שם אחד ורבי יהודה היא דמחייב אחלב מוקדשין שתים משום חלב ושני שמות דקתני משום דבחלב מוקדשין כתיבי תרי קראי:
notes.en: Rather, Rav Sheshet said: for example, where he ate fat of the sacred: and in fact it is on account of fat that he is liable to two; that is why the guilt offering for misuse is not counted, only [the sin offerings] of one name. And it is Rabbi Yehuda, who renders one liable to two for the fat of consecrated animals on account of fat; and the “two names” it teaches are because two verses are written concerning the fat of consecrated animals.

notes.dh: ור' יהודה אמר חלב מוקדשין לוקה שלש
notes.he: דקסבר תרוויהו לאוי בקדש כתיבי וחייב שלש. וכרבנן הוה יכיל רב ששת (יכיל) לתרוצי דאמרי חייב שתים בחלב דקדשים אבל הא דאוקמיה כר' יהודה משום דרבותא קמ"ל דר' יהודה מחייב אחלב שתים משום ב' לאוין והיינו ב' שמות בהעלם אחד:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehuda says: for fat of consecrated animals he is flogged three, since he holds that both prohibitions are written about the sacred, and he is liable to three. Rav Sheshet could have answered in accordance with the Rabbis, who say he is liable to two for the fat of sacrificial animals; but he established it according to Rabbi Yehuda because it teaches us a novelty: that Rabbi Yehuda renders one liable for fat twice on account of two prohibitions, and that is “two names in one lapse of awareness.”

messages.text: As it is taught in a baraita:

If one ate forbidden fat of an animal carcass, or if he ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, he is liable to receive two sets of lashes, either for transgressing the prohibitions of eating forbidden fat and eating an animal carcass, or for both eating forbidden fat and transgressing the prohibition forbidding a non-priest to partake of sacrificial animals.

notes.he: משום חלב ומשום נבלה והמוקדשין משום חלב ומשום זרות:
notes.en: Fat of a carcass, he is flogged two: on account of fat and on account of a carcass. And [fat of] consecrated animals: on account of fat and on account of a non-priest [eating sacred food].

notes.he: לוקה שתים אחת משום חלב ואחת משום נבלה:
notes.en: Fat of a carcass: he is flogged two, one on account of fat and one on account of a carcass.

notes.he: חלב מוקדשי' לוקה שתים אחד משום חלב ואחד משום קודש ואע"ג דכתיבי תרי לאוין בחלב קסברי רבנן לאו וכל חלב שור בחולין מיירי ולא בקדשים:
notes.en: Fat of consecrated animals: he is flogged two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred. And even though two prohibitions are written about fat, the Rabbis hold that the prohibition of “all fat of ox” speaks of non-sacred animals and not of sacrificial ones.

messages.text: If one ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals he is flogged with three sets of lashes, because there are two separate prohibitions of forbidden fat in the case of sacrificial animals, as the Gemara will soon explain, in addition to the prohibition forbidding a non-priest to partake of sacrificial animals.

notes.he: ב' משום חלב כדמפ' לקמן וא' משום זרות:
notes.en: Three: two on account of fat, as is explained below, and one on account of a non-priest.

messages.text: And let us interpret this baraita as referring to a case where he ate the forbidden fat of an ox, and of a sheep, and of a goat, and explain that it is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael, who says that he is flogged with three sets of lashes for the different types of fat, if he did so intentionally and was forewarned.
messages.lead: They laughed at this suggestion in the West, i.e., Eretz Yisrael:

notes.he: להא דלעיל דקתני ב' שמות כלומר משתי בהמות משני מינין ור' ישמעאל היא:
notes.en: And let us establish: the baraita above, which teaches “two names,” that is, from two animals of two species, as Rabbi Yishmael.

notes.dh: אי הכי אי משום רבותא קאמרת ונוקמא כר' ישמעאל דאמר דאחלב לוקה שלש
notes.he: וכי אכל ב' שמות לוקה שתים אלא אמאי לא אוקמא כו':
notes.en: If so, if you speak of a novelty, let us establish it according to Rabbi Yishmael, who says that for fat he is flogged three; and where he ate two names he is flogged two. Rather, why did he not establish it, etc.

messages.text: 4b
Why does one not interpret the baraita in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael?
messages.quote: it is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael

messages.text: Although Rabbi Yishmael maintains that one who eats the fat of an ox, a sheep, and a goat is liable to receive a separate set of lashes for each one, he would concede with regard to bringing an offering that if he ate those types of forbidden fat in a single lapse of awareness he is liable to bring only one sin offering.
messages.lead: The reason is as Rabbi Ḥanina says:

notes.he: וברייתא דלעיל בקרבן קמיירי דגבי חטאות כתיב ועשה מאחת מהנה:
notes.en: Regarding an offering: and the baraita above speaks of an offering, since regarding sin offerings it is written, “and does from one of them.”

messages.text: Now too, the baraita should not be interpreted in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, as doesn’t Rabbi Eliezer say: Rabbi Yehuda would concede with regard to bringing an offering that if one ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals he brings only one sin offering?

notes.he: אע"פ דלעיל אמר כ"מ שיש ב' לאוין וכרת אחת חילוק חטאות ביניהן היינו דוקא בב' דברים כגון סך ומפטם אבל בדבר אחד לא אמר חילוק:
notes.en: Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding an offering: even though it said above that wherever there are two prohibitions and one karet, the sin offerings are divided between them, that is only with two acts, such as smearing and compounding [the anointing oil]; but with one act he did not say there is a division.

notes.dh: השתא נמי כר' יהודה לא מיתוקמא דהא אמר כו'
notes.he: מאי רבותא קמ"ל ברייתא דחייב שתים:
notes.en: [A printer’s note: “Up to here belongs to 4a.”] Now too it cannot be established according to Rabbi Yehuda, since he said, etc. What novelty does the baraita teach us, that he is liable to two?

notes.he: מחכון עלה ואי רבותא קמ"ל נוקמא כגון דאכל חלב דשור וכשב ועז ור' ישמעאל היא דאמר לוקה שלש והאי דקתני חייב שתים דאכל שתים בלבד דשור וכשב אלא אמאי לא אוקמא כו'. דהא מודה שאינו חייב אלא חטאת אחת אחלב השתא נמי כר' יהודה כו' אלא ודאי אחת משום חלב ואחת משום קודש. והשתא נמי מיתוקמא כר' יהודה ברייתא ובין לרבנן ובין לר' ישמעאל למאי רבותא קמ"ל:
notes.en: They laughed at it: if it teaches us a novelty, let us establish it as where he ate fat of ox, sheep and goat, and it is Rabbi Yishmael, who says he is flogged three; and what it teaches, “liable to two,” is where he ate only two, of ox and sheep. Rather, why did he not establish it, etc.? Since he concedes that he is liable to only one sin offering for fat. Now too, according to Rabbi Yehuda, etc. Rather, certainly one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred. And now too the baraita can be established according to Rabbi Yehuda, and both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Yishmael; what novelty does it teach us?

messages.text: What are we dealing with here, where one is liable to bring two sin offerings for eating forbidden fat of two categories? We are dealing with a case in which he ate the forbidden fat from two dishes, i.e., where each part was prepared in a different manner, and this is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua, who says that dishes serve to separate the acts of eating. One who eats forbidden food from two different dishes in the course of a single lapse of awareness is considered to have transgressed two prohibitions and is liable to bring a sin offering for each one.
messages.lead: Rather, Reish Lakish said in the name of the Sage bar Ta’utni:
messages.quote: two categories, in one lapse of awareness

notes.he: הא דקתני ב' שמות כגון שאכלן בב' תמחוין ב' מאכלין דהיינו ב' שמות כגון תבשיל וצלי:
notes.en: What are we dealing with here: that which it teaches, “two names,” is where he ate them in two dishes, two foods, which are two names, such as a stew and a roast.

notes.he: (ל"א חייב ב' - א' משום חלב וא' משום קדש אשם מעילה ודלא כר' יהודה דמחייב משום חלב שתים משום ב' לאוין דכתיבי בחלב בתרי פסוקי):
notes.en: (Another version: he is liable to two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred, the guilt offering for misuse; and not like Rabbi Yehuda, who renders one liable twice on account of fat, on account of two prohibitions written about fat in two verses.)

notes.he: בפרק אמרו לו (לקמן כריתות טו:):
notes.en: Of Rabbi Yehoshua: in the chapter Amru Lo (below, Keritot 15b).

notes.he: הא קמ"ל כגון שאכלו ב' זיתי דחלב דחולין בב' תמחויין כלומר בב' תבשילין א' צלי וא' מבושל והיינו (קרי שמא) [שני שמות] ומשום הכי חייב שתים כדר' יהושע דאמר בהא מסכת בפרק אמרו לו. אמר ר' יהושע שמעתי באוכל מזבח אחד בחמשה תמחוין בהעלם אחד חייב על כל אחד [ואחד] משום מעילה קסבר תמחוין מחלקין:
notes.en: Reish Lakish said: This is what it teaches us: for example, where he ate two olive-bulks of fat of non-sacred animals in two dishes, that is, in two cooked foods, one roasted and one boiled, and these are two names. That is why he is liable to two, according to Rabbi Yehoshua, who said in this tractate, in the chapter Amru Lo: Rabbi Yehoshua said: I heard that one who eats from one offering in five dishes in one lapse of awareness is liable for each and every one on account of misuse; he holds that dishes separate.

notes.he: לישנא אחרינא כגון דאכל חלב דהקדש ורבותא קמ"ל דחייב שתים ודלא כר' יהודה דאמר שלש:
notes.en: Another version: for example, where he ate fat of consecrated property, and it teaches us a novelty: that he is liable to two, not like Rabbi Yehuda, who says three.

notes.he: דבהכי קא מיירי ברייתא כגון דאכלו בב' תמחויין ור' יהושע היא:
notes.en: Rather, Reish Lakish said: that the baraita deals with this, for example where he ate them in two dishes, and it is Rabbi Yehoshua.

messages.text: § The Gemara returns to discuss the matter itself:

If one ate forbidden fat of an animal carcass he is flogged with two sets of lashes for transgressing the prohibitions of eating forbidden fat and consuming an animal carcass. If he ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, he is flogged with two sets of lashes, for both eating forbidden fat and transgressing the prohibition forbidding a non-priest to partake of sacrificial animals.
If one ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, he is flogged with three sets of lashes.

@Rava Granted, according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, this is the meaning of the three verses that are written: “It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings, that you shall eat neither fat nor blood” (Leviticus 3:17); “You shall eat no fat, of ox, or sheep, or goat” (Leviticus 7:23); “And no non-priest shall partake of the sacred food” (Leviticus 22:10), as these are three prohibitions, two for eating forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, as the two verses that mention fat are discussing sacrificial animals, and one for the prohibition forbidding a non-priest to partake of consecrated food.

notes.he: חד בקדשים חוקת עולם וחד בין בחולין בין בקדשים הילכך בחלב המוקדשים איכא שני לאוין משום חלב וחלב חולין נפקא ליה לר' יהודה כדאמרינן בפ' אלו עוברין (פסחים מג:) כי כל אוכל חלב מן הבהמה אין לי אלא חלב תמימין הראוי ליקרב חלב בעלי מומין מנין תלמוד לומר כל חלב חולין מנין תלמוד לומר כי כל:
notes.en: Two verses: one about sacrificial animals, “a perpetual statute,” and one [applying] both to non-sacred and to sacrificial animals. Therefore with the fat of consecrated animals there are two prohibitions on account of fat. And Rabbi Yehuda derives the fat of non-sacred animals as we say in the chapter Elu Overin (Pesaḥim 43b): “For whoever eats the fat of the animal”: I have only the fat of unblemished animals, fit to be offered; the fat of blemished animals, from where? The verse states “whoever.” Non-sacred animals, from where? The verse states “for whoever.”

messages.text: But according to the opinion of the Rabbis, what is their reasoning? Why is one liable to receive only two sets of lashes?

The Rabbis maintain that the prohibition of: “It shall be a perpetual statute,” was stated with regard to sacrificial animals, but the prohibition of: “You shall eat no fat of ox,” was stated with regard to non-sacred animals. Therefore, if one ate forbidden fat of sacrificial animals he is liable to receive only two sets of lashes. And both verses are necessary, as one could not have been derived from the other.
messages.quote: according to the opinion of the Rabbis, what is their reasoning?

notes.dh: קסברי רבנן לאו דחקת עולם בקדשים
notes.he: דהא בעניינא דקדשים כתיב ולאו דכל חלב בחולין ולא בקדשים:
notes.en: The Rabbis hold the prohibition of “a perpetual statute” is about sacrificial animals: since it is written in the context of sacrificial animals; and the prohibition of “all fat” is about non-sacred animals and not sacrificial ones.

notes.he: בשלמא לר' יהודה היינו דכתיב תרי קראי בחלב וקסבר תרוייהו בקדשים כתיבי ורבנן סברי חד בחול קא מיירי ולא בקדשים הילכך אינו לוקה אלא שתים אחת משום חלב ואחת משום קודש:
notes.en: Granted according to Rabbi Yehuda: this is why two verses are written about fat, and he holds both are written about sacrificial animals. But the Rabbis hold one speaks of non-sacred animals and not of sacrificial ones; therefore he is flogged only two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred.

notes.he: חד בחולין חד בקדשים:
notes.en: And they are necessary: one for non-sacred animals, one for sacrificial animals.

messages.text: As, had the Merciful One written the prohibition against eating forbidden fat only with regard to sacrificial animals I would say: It is only in the case of sacrificial animals, whose prohibitions are generally stringent, that their fat is forbidden. But with regard to non-sacred animals one might say their fat is not forbidden. It is due to that reason that the Merciful One writes: “You shall eat no fat of ox.”

notes.dh: ה"ג אבל דחולין דאסור חלבו אימא לא
notes.he: והכי פירושא אבל חולין דקילי אימא לא אסיר חלבו. דאסור חלבו אימא לא כלומר אימא לא אסור חלבו ולשון הפוך היא לשון גרסא ירושלמית:
notes.en: This is the reading: “But non-sacred animals, whose fat is forbidden, say not.” Its explanation: but non-sacred animals, which are lenient, say their fat is not forbidden. “Whose fat is forbidden, say not” means: say its fat is not forbidden. It is an inverted expression, a turn of phrase of the Jerusalem reading.

notes.he: הוה אמינא חולין לא ילפי מיניה דהיינו טעמא דבקדשים אסור חלב משום דחמירי דאסורין לזרים הילכך חלבו אסור וחייבין עליו אבל חלב חולין דלא חמיר אימא (כלומר) איסורא בעלמא (אימא) דאית ביה אבל חייבין חטאת לא להכי כתב כל חלב שור וגו' דגם בחולין ליחייב:
notes.en: For had it written about sacrificial animals: I would say non-sacred animals are not derived from it, since the reason fat is forbidden with sacrificial animals is that they are stringent, being forbidden to non-priests; therefore their fat is forbidden and one is liable for it. But the fat of non-sacred animals, which are not stringent, say it carries a mere prohibition but one is not liable to a sin offering. That is why it wrote “all fat of ox,” etc., that with non-sacred animals too he is liable.

messages.text: And by contrast, had the Merciful One written only: “You shall eat no fat of ox,” I would say: It is only the fat of non-sacred animals that is forbidden, since there are no circumstances in which its general prohibition was permitted, i.e., those fats of domesticated animals are always forbidden.

But with regard to sacrificial animals, whose general prohibition was permitted in certain circumstances, i.e., with regard to the rest of its meat after the blood has been sprinkled, I would say that from the fact that their meat was permitted, their fat was permitted as well. Therefore, both verses are necessary, in order to teach that the prohibition against eating forbidden fat applies equally to sacrificial animals and non-sacred animals.

notes.he: דהא אליה איקרי חלב בכבש ואישתראי בשור ועז:
notes.en: Fat of consecrated animals was permitted from its general prohibition: since the tail is called fat in a sheep, and it was permitted in an ox and a goat.

notes.he: בחולין ולא בקדשים הוה אמינא חלב חולין הוא דאסור משום דלא הותר מכלל איסורו לא לגבוה ולא להדיוט אבל חלב דקדשים דהותר מכללו לגבוה (אלא) לאחר זריקה והותר נמי בשרן דקדשים מכלל איסורן לאחר זריקה אימא מדהותר בשרן הותר חלבן צריכא דאסור:
notes.en: And had it written: about non-sacred animals and not about sacrificial ones, I would say it is the fat of non-sacred animals that is forbidden, since it was not permitted from its general prohibition, neither for the Most High nor for an ordinary person. But the fat of sacrificial animals, which was permitted from its general prohibition for the Most High after the sprinkling, and whose meat too was permitted from its general prohibition after the sprinkling, say: since their meat was permitted, their fat was permitted. It is necessary [to teach] that it is forbidden.

notes.he: ואמר לן ר' איכא ספרי דכתיב בהו הכי הוה אמינא חולין הוא דאסירן חלבן דלא הותר מכללן כלומר חולין אין בהן היתר מכלל דלעולם מותרין. אבל חלב מוקדשין דהותרו מכללן דבשר עצמו לפני זריקה אסור לאחר זריקה מותר הוה אמינא מדהותר בשרו מכללו כו':
notes.en: And my teacher told us there are books in which it is written thus: “I would say it is non-sacred animals whose fat is forbidden, since it was not permitted from its general prohibition”; that is, non-sacred animals have no permission out of a general prohibition, since they are always permitted. “But the fat of consecrated animals, which were permitted from their general prohibition,” since the meat itself is forbidden before the sprinkling and permitted after the sprinkling, “I would say: since its meat was permitted from its general prohibition,” etc.

messages.text: And Rabbi Yehuda maintains that when it is written: “You shall eat no fat of ox,” it is also written with regard to the matter of sacrificial animals, as it is stated after the prohibition against eating forbidden fat: “For whoever eats the fat of the animal, of which men present an offering of fire to the Lord, even the soul that eats it shall be cut off from his people” (Leviticus 7:25), and this is derived by employing the hermeneutical principle: A matter is derived from its context.

notes.dh: ור' יהודה סבר כי כתיב נמי כו'
notes.he: כדאמרן לעיל:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that when it is written, etc.: as we said above.

notes.dh: ור' יהודה סבר כי כתיב נמי
notes.he: כל חלב שור בענינא דקדשים כתיב דהא איירי לעיל בקדשים ודבר למד מענינו ואלא מכלל דלית להו לרבנן דבר למד מעניינו אלא דכולי עלמא בעלמא אית להו דבר למד מעניינו והכא בהא פליגי ר' יהודה סבר למדין לאו כל חלב שור מלאו דחקת עולם וההוא לאו מכרת דמיירי בבהמה דקדשים ומה כרת לחלק על כל בהמה ובהמה אף הני לאוין לחלק הלכך לוקה שלש:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that when it is written: “all fat of ox” is written in the context of sacrificial animals, since it speaks of sacrificial animals above, and a matter is learned from its context. But then, by inference, the Rabbis do not hold “a matter is learned from its context”?
