Rather, in general everyone holds a matter is learned from its context, and here they disagree about this: Rabbi Yehuda holds we derive the prohibition of “all fat of ox” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” and that prohibition from the karet, which speaks of a sacrificial animal; and just as the karet is to separate for each and every animal, so too these prohibitions are to separate. Therefore he is flogged three.

messages.text: But can one conclude from here by inference that the Rabbis maintain we do not derive halakhot by employing the hermeneutical principle of: A matter is derived from its context? This cannot be correct, as it is an accepted, basic principle of exegesis.

notes.he: בתמיה:
notes.en: By inference the Rabbis do not derive: [said] in astonishment.

messages.text: No; everyone agrees we do derive halakhot by employing the hermeneutical principle of: A matter is derived from its context. And it is about this issue that they disagree: Rabbi Yehuda maintains that we derive the halakhot of one prohibition from the halakhot of another prohibition, and we derive the halakhot of a prohibition from the punishment of karet, and therefore he derives that the prohibition: “You shall eat no fat of ox,” is also written with regard to sacrificial animals from the nearby verse concerning karet, which is referring to sacrificial animals.
messages.quote: the Rabbis maintain we do not derive

notes.he: דבר מעניינו בין לאו מלאו כגון בעלמא גבי אבר מן חי בפ' (כל הבשר) (חולין קב.) בין לאו מכרת כגון הכא מה כרת בקדשים אף לאו בקדשים:
notes.en: We derive a prohibition from a prohibition and a prohibition from karet: a matter from its context; whether a prohibition from a prohibition, as elsewhere with a limb from a living animal in the chapter (Kol HaBasar) (Ḥullin 102a), or a prohibition from karet, as here: just as the karet is about sacrificial animals, so too the prohibition is about sacrificial animals.

messages.text: And the Rabbis maintain that generally we derive the halakhot of one prohibition from the halakhot of another prohibition, but we do not derive the halakhot of a prohibition from the punishment of karet, and one is liable to receive karet for eating forbidden fat of sacrificial animals.

notes.dh: ורבנן סברי לאו מלאו הוא דילפינן
notes.he: כי התם אבל לאו מכרת לא ילפינן הלכך בחולין כתיב. ואף בזו הספרים משובשים וכולה גרסא ליתא:
notes.en: And the Rabbis hold it is a prohibition from a prohibition that we derive: as there; but a prohibition from karet we do not derive. Therefore it is written about non-sacred animals. In this too the books are corrupt, and the whole [longer] reading does not belong.

notes.he: כל חלב שור בחולין הוא דכתיב ולאו מלאו ילפינן לאיסור בעלמא כדאמר לעיל דהיינו דבר למד מעניינו דדמי להו ללאו לאו מכרת לא ילפינן דלא דמי ליה הלכך לא מצית למילף מיניה לחלק ואינו לוקה אלא שתים. ור' יהודה דמוקים לתרי קראי בקדשים מרבי לחלב חולין מכל חלב שור דשמעינן לר' יהודה דדריש כל במס' זבחים ובין רבנן ובין ר' יהודה כרת לחלב דחולין נפקא להו מרבוי כי כל אוכל חלב דאפי' למאן דלא דריש כל כי כל דריש:
notes.en: And the Rabbis hold: “all fat of ox” is written about non-sacred animals, and we derive a prohibition from a prohibition for a mere prohibition, as it said above, that this is “a matter learned from its context,” since one prohibition resembles the other; a prohibition from karet we do not derive, since it does not resemble it. Therefore you cannot derive from it to separate, and he is flogged only two. And Rabbi Yehuda, who establishes both verses about sacrificial animals, includes the fat of non-sacred animals from “all fat of ox,” for we have heard that Rabbi Yehuda expounds “all” in tractate Zevaḥim. And both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda derive karet for the fat of non-sacred animals from the inclusion in “For whoever eats fat,” for even one who does not expound “all” expounds “for all.”

messages.text: But if so, then according to Rabbi Yehuda, for what purpose does the verse: “It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings, that you shall eat neither fat nor blood” (Leviticus 3:17), come? After all, he has already derived the prohibition against eating the forbidden fat of sacrificial animals from the verse: “You shall eat no fat of ox.”
He requires it to juxtapose the prohibition against consuming blood to the prohibition against eating forbidden fat. As it is taught in a baraita:

notes.he: ואלא לר' יהודה דמוקים תרוייהו בקדשים כל חלב וכל דם כל דם למאי אתא הלכך כתב הכא לומר לך מה חלב בקדשים לוקה שתים אף דם לוקה שתים להכי אקשיה לחלב:
notes.en: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who establishes both about sacrificial animals, [in] “all fat and all blood,” what does “all blood” come for? It was written here to tell you: just as for fat of sacrificial animals he is flogged two, so too for blood he is flogged two. That is why it juxtaposed it to fat.

messages.text: “You shall eat neither fat nor blood,” which teaches that just as for eating forbidden fat one is flogged with two sets of lashes, so too, for eating blood one is flogged with two sets of lashes. This is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

notes.he: ה"ג ת"ר כל חלב וכל דם לא תאכלו ר' יהודה אומר מה חלב לוקה שתים אף דם לוקה שתים וחכ"א אין בו אלא אזהרה אחת:
notes.en: This is the reading: The Sages taught: “All fat and all blood you shall not eat.” Rabbi Yehuda says: Just as for fat he is flogged two, so too for blood he is flogged two. And the Rabbis say: There is only one warning in it.

messages.text: Only one prohibition applies to blood.

Why is the juxtaposition necessary according to Rabbi Yehuda? And what is different about forbidden fat that the baraita states that one who eats it is flogged with two sets of lashes even without needing to derive the double punishment from a juxtaposition? The reason must be that two verses are written with regard to it: “You shall eat neither fat nor blood,” and: “You shall eat no fat of ox or sheep.”
messages.quote: so too, for eating blood one is flogged with two sets of lashes

notes.he: כלומר מ"ט כתביה לדם בהדי חלב ליכתביה באנפי נפשיה ואנא ידענא דלוקה ב' דמ"ש חלב דלוקה שתים בלא הקישא כלומר דם נמי כתיבי ב' קראי אי הוה כתיב באנפי נפשיה כגון כל דם לא תאכלו לכתוב בחקת עולם ל"ל דכתיב בהדי חלב:
notes.en: What is different about fat: that is, why did it write blood together with fat? Let it write it on its own, and I would know he is flogged two. For what is different about fat, that he is flogged two without the juxtaposition? That is, blood too has two verses written, if it were written on its own, such as “You shall eat no blood”; why does it need to be written in “a perpetual statute” together with fat?

notes.he: דפשיטא ליה דלוקה שתים בלא היקשא כלומר דלא צריך היקשא משום דכתיבי ביה תרי קראי כו':
notes.en: What is different about fat: that it is obvious to him that he is flogged two without a juxtaposition; that is, it needs no juxtaposition, because two verses are written about it, etc.

messages.text: With regard to blood as well, even without deriving the halakha from a juxtaposition, one who consumes it should be flogged with two sets of lashes, as two prohibitions are written with regard to it: “You shall eat neither fat nor blood,” and the verse: “And you shall eat no manner of blood, whether it is of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwellings.”

verse.he: וְכׇל־דָּם לֹא תֹאכְלוּ בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם לָעוֹף וְלַבְּהֵמָה׃
verse.en: And you must not consume any blood, either of bird or of animal, in any of your settlements.

messages.text: Rather, say that the baraita states the following: The juxtaposition teaches that just as for eating forbidden fat one is flogged with three sets of lashes, two for eating forbidden fat of sacrificial animals and one for the prohibition of a non-priest partaking of sacrificial food, from the verse: “And no non-priest shall partake of the sacred food” (Leviticus 22:10), so too, for eating blood one is flogged with three sets of lashes.

And what is different about forbidden fat that it is obvious that one who eats it is flogged with three sets of lashes? The reason must be that these two prohibitions are written with regard to it, and there is also the prohibition of a non-priest partaking of consecrated food, as explained earlier, which totals three. The same can be said with regard to blood as well: The two verses stated above, together with the prohibition of a non-priest partaking of consecrated food, likewise render one liable to receive three sets of lashes. If so, the juxtaposition is unnecessary.

notes.he: תימה ל"ל למימר בלאו דזרות בלא"ה משכחת ביה דחד כתיב ביה בהדיא כל דם לא תאכלו בכל מושבותיכם ומן היקישא יש עוד שנים מה חלב לוקה ב' אף דם כו' וא"כ בלא זרות איכא תלתא:
notes.en: Blood too should be flogged three: This is puzzling: why does he need to say this with the prohibition of a non-priest? Even without it one finds three for it: one is written about it explicitly, “And you shall eat no manner of blood in any of your dwellings,” and from the juxtaposition there are two more, “just as fat is flogged two, so too blood,” etc. If so, there are three without the prohibition of a non-priest.

messages.text: The juxtaposition was necessary, as it might enter your mind to say: Since blood is excluded from the halakha of ritual impurity, as one who consumes the blood of sacrificial animals in a state of ritual impurity has not transgressed the prohibition against consuming sacrificial food while impure, let it also be excluded from the prohibition of consumption as a non-priest. To counter this, Rabbi Yehuda teaches us that it is derived from the juxtaposition that one receives three sets of lashes for consuming the blood of sacrificial animals, including for transgressing the prohibition of a non-priest.

notes.he: דם אימעיט ממעילה בסוף כל הבשר בשחיטת חולין (דף קיז:) ואימא כי היכי דאימעיט מזרות קרבן מעילה אימעיט נמי ממלקות דזרות קמ"ל:
notes.en: Blood is excluded from misuse, at the end of Kol HaBasar in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (117b). One might say: just as it was excluded from the guilt offering for misuse, so too it is excluded from lashes for a non-priest [eating it]. It teaches us [otherwise]. [Rashi reads “misuse” where the daf has “ritual impurity.”]

notes.he: ה"ג ס"ד אמינא הואיל ואימעיט ממעילה אימעיט נמי מזרות קמ"ל:
notes.en: This is the reading: “It might enter your mind to say: since it was excluded from misuse, it is also excluded from [the prohibition of] a non-priest; it teaches us [otherwise].”

notes.he: להכי אתא היקשא דסד"א הואיל ואיתמעיט (בסימן) מטומאה כדגרסינן בסיפי' דכל בשר. תלתא קראי בדם למה לי לכם לכפר הוא חד למעוטי מנותר וחד למעוטי ממעילה וחד למעוטי מטומא' איתמעט נמי מן לאו דזרות:
notes.en: Rather, say: this is why the juxtaposition comes, for it might enter your mind: since it was excluded from impurity, as we learn at the end of Kol HaBasar, “Why do I need three verses about blood? ‘To you… to atone’: one to exclude it from notar, one to exclude it from misuse and one to exclude it from impurity,” it is also excluded from the prohibition of a non-priest.

messages.caption: How many sets of lashes, as the daf counts them, for forbidden fat and for blood.

messages.text: But according to the Rabbis, who maintain that only one prohibition applies to the consumption of the blood of sacrificial animals and that one is not liable to receive lashes for partaking of it as a non-priest, for what purpose does this juxtaposition come?

notes.he: כיון דתרצינן דלר' יהודה לא בעי הקישא אלא משום זרות ורבנן פליגי עליה ואמרי אין בו אלא אזהרה אחת מכלל דסבירא להו מזרות נמי אימעיט ולדידהו הקישא ל"ל:
notes.en: But according to the Rabbis: since we answered that according to Rabbi Yehuda the juxtaposition is needed only on account of [the prohibition of] a non-priest, and the Rabbis disagree with him and say there is only one warning in it, by inference they hold it is excluded from [the prohibition of] a non-priest as well. So according to them, why do I need the juxtaposition?

notes.he: דסברי דאינו לוקה אלא אחת משום חלב היקשא למאי אתא:
notes.en: But according to the Rabbis: who hold he is flogged only once, on account of fat [so the text; the subject is blood], what does the juxtaposition come for?

notes.he: לישנא אחרינא בשלמא לר' יהודה דדריש ליה להאי קרא כל חלב וכל דם להיקשא שפיר דתניא כל חלב וכל דם וגו' וחכ"א אינו אלא באזהרה בלאו אחד אלא לרבנן היקשא למאי אתא מיתבעי ליה כו':
notes.en: Another version: Granted according to Rabbi Yehuda, who expounds this verse “all fat and all blood” for the juxtaposition, well and good, as it is taught: “All fat and all blood,” etc.; and the Rabbis say there is only a warning in it, one prohibition. But according to the Rabbis, what does the juxtaposition come for? It is needed, etc.

messages.text: They require it for that which is taught in a baraita:
messages.quote: for what purpose does this juxtaposition come?

messages.text: The verse states: “You shall eat neither fat nor blood,” which teaches that just as forbidden fat is unique in that the fat of the animal is discrete from its flesh, i.e., the fat is forbidden and the flesh is permitted, and therefore they do not combine with each other, i.e., if one ate half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat and half an olive-bulk of permitted meat he is not liable for eating an olive-bulk of forbidden food,

notes.dh: מה חלב מיוחד שחלבו חלוק מבשרו
notes.he: שלא נאמר איסור חלב אלא בשור וכשב ועז שחלבן אסור ובשרן מותר:
notes.en: Just as fat is unique in that its fat is distinct from its flesh: since the prohibition of fat is stated only for ox, sheep and goat, whose fat is forbidden and whose flesh is permitted.

notes.he: לאיסור שבה שהרי אין כאן אלא איסור החלב לבדו ואין היתר מצטרף לאיסור חוץ מאיסורי נזיר:
notes.en: And they do not combine with each other: for its prohibition, since there is only the prohibition of fat by itself here, and the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, except with the prohibitions of a nazirite.

messages.text: so too, the prohibition concerning blood does not combine with the flesh of non-kosher animals to constitute the volume of an olive-bulk in the case of an animal whose blood is discrete from its flesh, as the penalty of karet applies only to the animal’s blood, whereas its flesh is prohibited by a standard prohibition.

notes.he: אע"פ שאיסורו נוהג בטמאין וראוי להצטרף הדם והבשר להתחייב בכזית משניהן משום טמא לא יצטרפו שנלמד דם מחלב מה החלב על כרחיה לחלקו מפרידו מלהצטרף שהרי חלוקין זה לאיסור וזה להיתר דאין איסור והיתר מצטרפים אף דם הטמאים הואיל ודמן חלוק מבשרן שיש על הדם איסור כרת משום דם מה שאין כן בבשר אינו מצטרף אפילו לענין (איסור) לטמא:
notes.en: So too blood: even though its prohibition applies to non-kosher animals, so that the blood and the flesh would be fit to combine to make one liable for an olive-bulk of both on account of a non-kosher animal, they do not combine. For blood is learned from fat: just as with fat, its being distinct necessarily keeps it from combining, since they are distinct, one forbidden and one permitted, and the forbidden and the permitted do not combine; so too the blood of non-kosher animals, since their blood is distinct from their flesh, in that the blood carries a karet prohibition on account of blood, which is not so with the flesh, does not combine even with regard to the [prohibition of a] non-kosher [animal].

notes.he: לכדתניא דאמר מה חלב מיוחד שחלבו חלוק מבשרו שהחלב אסור ובשר מותר ואינו מצטרף זה עם זה שאם אכל חצי זית חלב וחצי זית בשר אין מצטרפין זה עם זה דכל איסורין שבתור' אין היתר מצטרף לאיסור ואפי' בקדשים נמי אין היתר מצטרף לאיסור כדקתני ר' יהושע אמר כל הזבחים שבתורה נשתייר מהן כזית בשר כזית חלב זורק את הדם כחצי זית בשר כחצי זית חלב אין זורק את הדם. אף כל שדמו חלוק מבשרו אין מצטרף (אההוא) [ואינו] חייב אוציא דם שרצים שאין דמם חלוק מבשרן דזה וזה אסורין באכילה ומצטרף זה עם זה כדתנן במס' מעילה (דף יז) דם השרץ ובשרו מצטרפין לכעדשה. וקא ילפי מהיקשא דדם שרץ ובשרו מצטרף:
notes.en: For that which is taught, which says: just as fat is unique in that its fat is distinct from its flesh, the fat forbidden and the flesh permitted, and they do not combine with each other, so that if he ate half an olive-bulk of fat and half an olive-bulk of meat they do not combine (for with all the prohibitions in the Torah the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, and even with sacrificial animals the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, as Rabbi Yehoshua taught: With all the offerings in the Torah, if an olive-bulk of meat or an olive-bulk of fat remained of them, he sprinkles the blood; half an olive-bulk of meat and half an olive-bulk of fat, he does not sprinkle the blood), so too whatever’s blood is distinct from its flesh does not combine, and he is not liable. I will exclude the blood of creeping animals, whose blood is not distinct from their flesh, since both are forbidden to eat, and they combine with each other, as we learned in tractate Me’ila (17a): The blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine for a lentil-bulk. And they derive from the juxtaposition that the blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine. [An editor’s note: all this is cited in the Arukh, entry dam 3.]

messages.text: Accordingly, I will exclude from this halakha the blood of the carcasses of creeping animals, since their blood is not discrete from their flesh, i.e., no separate prohibition applies to the blood of creeping animals, and consequently their flesh and blood combine with each other to form the volume of an olive-bulk of a creeping animal.

notes.he: מדין ההיקש הזה הואיל ואין דמן חלוק מבשרן שאינו מוזהר על דמן משום דם אלא משום שרץ כדאמרי' בפר' דם שחיטה (לקמן כריתות כא:) יצאו שרצים שאין בהן טומאה קלה כו' הילכך מצטרפין זה עם זה שהרי שם אחד להן הילכך דם נחש ובשרו מצטרפין דאין מוזהר על דמן משום דם כדאמרינן בפרק דם שחיטה (שם) שאין אזהרת דם אלא בבהמה חיה ועוף כו':
notes.en: Creeping animals are excluded: from the rule of this juxtaposition, since their blood is not distinct from their flesh, as one is not warned about their blood on account of blood but on account of a creeping animal, as we say in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (below, Keritot 21b): “Creeping animals are excluded, which have no light impurity,” etc. Therefore they combine with each other, since they have one name. Therefore the blood of a snake and its flesh combine, since one is not warned about their blood on account of blood, as we say in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (there), that the warning about blood applies only to domesticated animals, undomesticated animals and birds, etc.

messages.text: But is this halakha derived from here, i.e., from the derivation from the verse: “You shall eat neither fat nor blood”? It is derived from there, from a different verse, as it is taught in a baraita:
messages.quote: their flesh and blood combine

notes.he: דאי ללמוד לשרץ גופיה הא כתיב אלה הטמאים לכם:
notes.en: The blood of a creeping animal is derived from “And this”: for if it came to teach about the creeping animal itself, it is already written, “These are the impure for you.”

messages.text: The verse states: “And these are they that are impure for you among the creeping animals.” This teaches with regard to the blood of one of the eight creeping animals listed in the Torah and the flesh of the creeping animal, that they combine with each other to constitute the minimum volume.

verse.he: וְזֶה לָכֶם הַטָּמֵא בַּשֶּׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל־הָאָרֶץ הַחֹלֶד וְהָעַכְבָּר וְהַצָּב לְמִינֵהוּ׃
verse.en: The following shall be impure for you from among the things that swarm on the earth: the mole, the mouse, and great lizards of every variety;

notes.he: הא מן וזה לכם הטמא לימד על דם השרצים ובשרו שמצטרף דמייתר הוא דהא כתיב ואלה הטמאים לכם בכל השרץ:
notes.en: But from “and this is impure for you” it was taught about the blood of creeping animals and their flesh that they combine, since it is superfluous, as it is written, “and these are the impure for you among all the creeping animals.”

messages.text: If not for the juxtaposition, it might enter your mind to say this statement applies with regard to ritual impurity, that the blood of one of the creeping animals listed in the Torah and its flesh combine with each other to constitute the lentil-bulk measure required to impart impurity. But with regard to consumption, one might say they do not combine with each other. Therefore, the juxtaposition teaches us that they combine even with regard to consumption.

notes.he: לכעדשה:
notes.en: For impurity: for a lentil-bulk.

notes.he: בכזית:
notes.en: For eating: for an olive-bulk.

notes.he: דחמיר דשיעורו בכעדשה אבל לענין אכילה דבכזית אימא לא תימה דנימא הקישא ונשתוק מוזה לכם הטמא ולגמר טומאה מאכילה:
notes.en: That applies to impurity: which is stringent, as its measure is a lentil-bulk; but with eating, which is an olive-bulk, say not. This is puzzling: let us state the juxtaposition and do without “And this is impure for you,” and derive impurity from eating.

notes.he: סד"א מן וזה לכם הטמא יליף דמצטרף לטומאה אבל לאכול אימא לא מצטרף לחייבי מלקות קמ"ל היקשא דמצטרף:
notes.en: It might enter your mind: from “and this is impure for you” one derives that it combines for impurity, but for eating, say it does not combine to make one liable to lashes. The juxtaposition teaches us that it combines.

messages.text: Therefore, the blood of a snake and its flesh combine with each other to constitute the volume of an olive-bulk.

notes.he: דאמרת כל שאין דמו חלוק מבשרו מצטרפין:
notes.en: Therefore: since you said that whatever’s blood is not distinct from its flesh combines.

notes.he: אע"ג דלאו בר טומאה הוא מצטרף דמו לבשרו לכזית לאכילה דאין מוזהרין על דמו אלא משום בשרו:
notes.en: A snake too: even though it is not subject to impurity, its blood combines with its flesh for an olive-bulk for eating, since one is warned about its blood only on account of its flesh.

notes.he: הואיל וכך דאמרת שאין דמו חלוק מבשרו מצטרף דם נחש ובשרו אע"ג דאינה משמונה שרצים מצטרף:
notes.en: Ravina said: since it is so, that you said whatever’s blood is not distinct from its flesh combines, the blood of a snake and its flesh combine, even though it is not one of the eight creeping animals.

messages.text: What is Ravina teaching us? This is exactly the derivation from the juxtaposition.
messages.quote: the blood of a snake and its flesh combine

notes.he: רבינא היינו היקשא דמה לי שרץ ובשרו מה לי נחש ובשרו:
notes.en: What does he teach us: Ravina? That is the juxtaposition, for what difference is there between a creeping animal and its flesh and a snake and its flesh?

messages.text: It might enter your mind to say that with regard to a creeping animal, whose blood is included with regard to ritual impurity, it is also included with regard to consumption; whereas a snake, whose blood is not included with regard to ritual impurity, as it is not one of the eight creeping animals that are ritually impure (see Leviticus 11:29–30), is not included with regard to consumption. Therefore, the juxtaposition teaches us that every item whose blood is not discrete from its flesh is included in the derivation that its blood and flesh combine with each other.

notes.he: כדאמרן וזה לכם הטמא לימד על דם השרץ ובשרו שמצטרפין לטומאה:
notes.en: Which were included for impurity: as we said, “And this is impure for you” taught that the blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine for impurity.

notes.he: אצטריך דרבינא ואיצטריך היקשא סד"א שרץ הוא דאיתרבי לטומאה כדכתיב וזה לכם הטמא הואיל ומצטרף לטומאה מצטרף לאכילה אבל נחש דלא דאיתרבי לטומאה דלא מטמא קמ"ל היקשא כו':
notes.en: Ravina’s statement was needed, and the juxtaposition was needed: it might enter your mind that it is the creeping animal that was included for impurity, as it is written, “and this is impure for you”; since it combines for impurity, it combines for eating. But a snake, which was not included for impurity, since it does not impart impurity, [would not]. The juxtaposition teaches us, etc.

messages.text: § Concerning the three mentions of karet that are stated with regard to blood (Leviticus 7:27, 17:10, 17:14), about what types of blood do they teach? One is for the blood of non-sacred animals, one is for the blood of sacrificial animals, and one is for the blood of exudate, i.e., which exudes from the neck of the animal after the initial spurt of its slaughter.

notes.he: תרין באחרי מות וחד בצו את אהרן:
notes.en: Three karet penalties: two in [the portion of] Aḥarei Mot and one in Tzav et Aharon.

notes.he: למה אחת בפרשה צו את אהרן ושנים בפרשה אחרי מות:
notes.en: Three karet penalties regarding blood: why? One in the portion Tzav et Aharon and two in the portion Aḥarei Mot.

messages.text: This works out well according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, as it is taught in a baraita:
messages.quote: and one is for the blood of exudate

messages.text: There is a prohibition stated with regard to the blood of exudate, but one is not punished with karet for consuming it. This is not as severe as consuming regular blood, for which one is liable to receive karet.
One is liable to receive karet for the blood of exudate, as this blood is regarded as full-fledged blood.
But according to the opinion of the Rabbis, who say there is no punishment of karet for consuming blood of exudate, for what purpose does that third mention of karet concerning blood come?
And even according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, he derives the karet that one receives for this blood from a different source, from the superfluous phrase: “Who eats any manner of blood.”

verse.he: וְאִישׁ אִישׁ מִבֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמִן־הַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכָם אֲשֶׁר יֹאכַל כׇּל־דָּם וְנָתַתִּי פָנַי בַּנֶּפֶשׁ הָאֹכֶלֶת אֶת־הַדָּם וְהִכְרַתִּי אֹתָהּ מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּהּ׃
verse.en: And regarding anyone of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who reside among them, who partakes of any blood: I will set My face against the person who partakes of the blood; I will cut them off from among their kin.

notes.he: לא נפקא ליה דם התמצית מחד מהנך כריתות:
notes.en: And even according to Rabbi Yehuda: he does not derive the blood of exudate from one of these karet penalties.

messages.text: As it is taught in a baraita concerning the verse: “And whatever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among them, that eats any manner of blood, I will set My face against that soul that eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people,” that
The verse could have stated in the first part of the verse: That eats blood. What is the meaning when the verse states there: “That eats any manner of blood”?

notes.he: הוה ליה למיכתב:
notes.en: “Blood”: it should have written.

notes.he: באחרי מות איש איש מבית ישראל ומן הגר הגר בתוכם אשר יאכל כל דם ונתתי פני וגו' אין לי שיהא בכרת אלא דם קדשים שהנפש יוצאה בו שמתכפר בו שראוי לכפרה על המזבח דהא כפרה כתיבא הכא ואני נתתיו לכם על המזבח לכפר והני הוא דראויין לכפרה:
notes.en: What does the verse teach with “any blood”: in Aḥarei Mot: “Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who eats any blood, I will set My face…”. I have [karet] only for the blood of sacrificial animals with which the soul goes out, through which atonement is achieved, which is fit for atonement on the altar, since atonement is written here, “and I have given it to you upon the altar to atone,” and these are the ones fit for atonement.

messages.text: I have derived only the punishment of karet concerning the blood of sacrificial animals with regard to which the soul of the animal leaves the body when it emerges, as atonement is achieved through this blood, and the next verse states: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls.”

verse.he: כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם הִוא וַאֲנִי נְתַתִּיו לָכֶם עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ לְכַפֵּר עַל־נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם כִּי־הַדָּם הוּא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ יְכַפֵּר׃
verse.en: For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have assigned it to you for making expiation for your lives upon the altar; it is the blood, as life, that effects expiation.

notes.he: עיקר דם קדשים שהנפש יוצא בו שמכפר כדכתיב כי הדם בנפש יכפר:
notes.en: I have only: principally the blood of sacrificial animals, with which the soul goes out, which atones, as it is written, “for it is the blood that atones by reason of the life.”

messages.text: From where do I derive that the same punishment of karet applies to the blood of a non-sacred animal and the blood of exudate? The verse states: “Any manner of blood.”

notes.he: לקדשים דאינם ראוין לכפרה כדאמרינן בסוף תמיד נשחט בפסחים (דף סה.):
notes.en: Blood of non-sacred animals and blood of exudate: of sacrificial animals, which are not fit for atonement, as we say at the end of Tamid Nishḥat in Pesaḥim (65a).

notes.he: ת"ל כל דם דם חולין דהכא לאו דווקא נסיב ליה דבדם חולין בפירוש אשכחן כרת דכתיב אשר יצוד וגו' אלא ואחד לדם כסוי הדם חיה ועוף בין לר' יהודה ובין לרבנן:
notes.en: The blood of non-sacred animals and the blood of exudate, from where? The verse states, “any blood.” The blood of non-sacred animals is not meant precisely here, since for the blood of non-sacred animals we find karet explicitly, as it is written, “who hunts,” etc. Rather, [the third is] one for the blood of covering, the blood of an undomesticated animal or bird, both according to Rabbi Yehuda and according to the Rabbis.

messages.text: Rava’s statement, that the punishment of karet for consuming blood of exudate is derived from a different verse, does not accord with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda either.

Rather, say that this is what Rava means: One mention of karet is for the blood of non-sacred animals, and one is for the blood of sacrificial animals, and one is for the blood of covering, i.e., the blood of an undomesticated animal or a bird, with regard to which there is a mitzva to cover their blood (see Leviticus 17:13).
messages.quote: three mentions of karet that are stated with regard to blood

notes.he: לעולם רבנן דלא נפקא לחולין מריבויא דקרא דכל ואע"ג דלית להו כרת בדם התמצית מיבעי להו חד כרת לדם כיסוי לדם חיה ועוף שכיסהו ונתגלה סד"א בטלה אגב ארעא ואי הדר אכלה עפרא בעלמא הוא ולא ליחייב קמ"ל:
notes.en: Rather: in fact [this is according to] the Rabbis, who do not derive non-sacred blood from the inclusive word “any.” Even though they do not hold there is karet for the blood of exudate, they need one karet for the blood of covering: the blood of an undomesticated animal or bird that one covered and it became uncovered. It might enter your mind to say it was nullified to the ground, and if he then ate it, it is mere dust and he should not be liable. It teaches us [otherwise].

notes.he: ולר' יהודה נמי חד לקדשים ודם התמצית וחד לדם חולין וחד לדם כסוי וברייתא דקתני דם חולין ודם התמצית מנין לאו דוקא דליהוי תרווייהו מחד קרא דכל:
notes.en: Rather, say one for non-sacred blood: and according to Rabbi Yehuda too: one for sacrificial blood and the blood of exudate, one for the blood of non-sacred animals, and one for the blood of covering. And the baraita that teaches “the blood of non-sacred animals and the blood of exudate, from where?” is not meant precisely, as though both came from the one verse “any.”

notes.he: איצטריך קרא דלא נימא לא תאכלנו על הארץ תשפכנו כמים דמשמע הא אין נשפך אין חייבין עליו קמ"ל:
notes.en: For the blood of covering: the verse was needed so that we not say [from] “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth like water,” which implies that what is not poured out, one is not liable for. It teaches us [otherwise].

messages.text: And further: Why are there five prohibitions stated with regard to blood (Leviticus 3:17, 7:26, 17:14; Deuteronomy 12:16–23)? One is for the blood of non-sacred animals, and one is for the blood of sacrificial animals, and one is for the blood of covering, and one is for the blood left in the limbs of the animal, and one is for the blood of exudate.

notes.he: הנך דלא אתו לדרשה חד (ויקרא ג׳:י״ז) דחקת עולם וחד בצו את אהרן (שם ז) כל דם לא תאכלו בכל מושבותיכם וחד באחרי מות (שם יז) דם כל בשר לא תאכלו וחד בראה אנכי (דברים י״ב:ט״ז) לא תאכלו על הארץ תשפכנו כמים הרי ה' ודכתיב לעיל מיניה לא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר באבר מן החי משתעי ודכתיב בתריה לא תאכלנו מוקמינן בפרק כל הבשר בשחיטת חולין (דף קטו:) אזהרה לבשר בחלב ועוד כתיב בראה אנכי רק את דמו לא תאכלו ומוקמינן ליה בפרק שני דבכורות (דף טו.) לחלב פסולי המוקדשים ודכתיב באחרי מות כל נפש מכם לא תאכל דם מוקים ליה תורת כהנים להזהיר גדולים על הקטנים:
notes.en: Five prohibitions: those that do not come for another exposition: one (Leviticus 3:17), “a perpetual statute”; one in Tzav et Aharon (Leviticus 7[:26]), “And you shall eat no manner of blood in any of your dwellings”; one in Aḥarei Mot (Leviticus 17[:14]), “You shall not eat the blood of any flesh”; and one in Re’eh (Deuteronomy 12:16), “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth like water.” That makes five. And that which is written before it, “You shall not eat the life with the flesh,” speaks of a limb from a living animal; and that which is written after it, “You shall not eat it,” we establish in the chapter Kol HaBasar in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (115b) as a warning against meat in milk. It is also written in Re’eh, “Only you shall not eat its blood,” which we establish in the second chapter of Bekhorot (15a) as about the milk of disqualified consecrated animals. And what is written in Aḥarei Mot, “No soul of you shall eat blood,” Torat Kohanim establishes as warning adults concerning minors.

notes.he: הכתובין בדם לאו דחוקת עולם ולאו דכל חלב שור וכשב ועז לא תאכלו ושלשה בפרשת אחרי מות אחד לדם חולין כו' לדם האברים שיוצא מן האברים כשחותכין אותן (אחר) [קודם] שחיטה דהוי אבר מן החי ועוד יש בו ארבעה לאוין בדם והן לדרשה באין אחד ואליהם תאמר איש וגו' אתי להזהיר בני ישראל קטנים על הגדולים שיפרישם מדם ורק את דמו לא תאכלו דבכור מוקמינן בבכורות מאי דמו חלבו דפסולי המוקדשין. ולא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר אתי למיסר דם מן החי דם הקזה שהנשמה יוצאה בו. ולא תאכלנו על הארץ תשפכנו אתי לבשר בחלב כדאמר בפ' כל הבשר האוכל מעשר שני אלו ג' מינין בחוץ דגן ותירוש ויצהר לוקה ג' משום דכתיב לא תוכל לאכל בשעריך וגו':
notes.en: Five prohibitions: written about blood: the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” and the prohibition of “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat” [so the text], and three in the portion Aḥarei Mot: one for the blood of non-sacred animals, etc.; for the blood of the limbs, which comes out of the limbs when they are cut (after) [before] slaughter, which is a limb from a living animal. And there are four more prohibitions about blood, and they come for expositions: “And you shall say to them, any man,” etc., comes to warn adult Israelites concerning minors, that they keep them from blood; “Only you shall not eat its blood,” of a firstborn, we establish in Bekhorot: what is “its blood”? Its milk, of disqualified consecrated animals; “You shall not eat the life with the flesh” comes to forbid blood from a living animal, the blood of bloodletting with which the soul goes out; and “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth” comes for meat in milk, as it says in the chapter Kol HaBasar. One who eats second tithe of these three kinds outside, grain, wine and oil, is flogged three, because it is written, “You may not eat within your gates,” etc.

messages.text: § If one ate outside Jerusalem the second tithe of grain, wine, and oil, he is flogged with three sets of lashes (see Deuteronomy 12:17).

notes.he: שני של דגן ותירוש ויצהר לוקה ג' משום לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך וגו':
notes.en: Rabbi Illa said: one who ate [second] tithe of grain, wine and oil is flogged three: on account of “You may not eat within your gates…”.

messages.text: But one is not flogged for transgressing a general prohibition. The prohibition concerning consuming second tithe outside Jerusalem is a general one, as it includes all of these categories.
messages.quote: he is flogged with three sets of lashes

messages.text: It is different here, as the verses are superfluous.

Since the Merciful One writes: “And you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place where He shall choose to cause His name to dwell there, the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil,” from which it is derived that inside the chosen place, Jerusalem, yes, one may eat second tithe, but outside Jerusalem, no, one may not eat second tithe;

verse.he: וְאָכַלְתָּ לִפְנֵי ׀ יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בַּמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר־יִבְחַר לְשַׁכֵּן שְׁמוֹ שָׁם מַעְשַׂר דְּגָנְךָ תִּירֹשְׁךָ וְיִצְהָרֶךָ וּבְכֹרֹת בְּקָרְךָ וְצֹאנֶךָ לְמַעַן תִּלְמַד לְיִרְאָה אֶת־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ כׇּל־הַיָּמִים׃
verse.en: You shall consume the tithes of your new grain and wine and oil, and the firstlings of your herds and flocks, in the presence of the ETERNAL your God, in the place where [God] will choose to establish the divine name, so that you may learn to revere the ETERNAL your God forever.

messages.text: why do I need the Merciful One to write: “You may not eat within your gates the tithe of your grain, or of your wine, or of your oil”? This verse serves to separate the prohibitions concerning tithes, to teach that one is separately liable to receive lashes for consuming each type of produce.

verse.he: לֹא־תוּכַל לֶאֱכֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ מַעְשַׂר דְּגָנְךָ וְתִירֹשְׁךָ וְיִצְהָרֶךָ וּבְכֹרֹת בְּקָרְךָ וְצֹאנֶךָ וְכׇל־נְדָרֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר תִּדֹּר וְנִדְבֹתֶיךָ וּתְרוּמַת יָדֶךָ׃
verse.en: You may not partake in your settlements of the tithes of your new grain or wine or oil, or of the firstlings of your herds and flocks, or of any of the votive offerings that you vow, or of your freewill offerings, or of your contributions.

messages.text: If the halakha were derived only from that verse, i.e., “And you shall eat before the Lord your God,” I would say this statement applies only to the extent that there is a prohibition derived by inference from a positive mitzva, for which one does not receive lashes, as it has the status of a positive mitzva. But one might say that one does not transgress a prohibition. It is due to this…

notes.he: לאו הבא מכלל עשה עשה:
notes.en: With a positive mitzva: a prohibition that comes by inference from a positive mitzva is [treated as] a positive mitzva.

notes.he: ואכלת הוה אמינא הני מילי בעשה הוא עובר דהיינו לאו הבא מכלל עשה עשה:
notes.en: If from that one: “And you shall eat,” I would say this applies only in that he transgresses a positive mitzva; that is, a prohibition that comes by inference from a positive mitzva is a positive mitzva.

messages.text: Continued on 5a: …reason that the Merciful One writes “You may not eat,” to establish eating second-tithe produce outside Jerusalem as a prohibition.
